items.sum: Report by T. J. Flower of the Club 10 Miles Cross Country Championship, run in terrible weather with the Brook in flood, won by Jim Ginty from holder Arthur Penny by about seven yards, with full result and handicap times.
items.s: THE 10 MILES CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report by T. J. Flower of the Club 10 Miles Cross Country Championship, run in terrible weather with the Brook in flood, won by Jim Ginty from holder Arthur Penny by about seven yards, with full result and handicap times. Although the weather was terrible, a good field turned out for this event. Arthur Penny, the holder, was looking very fit and confident, as were quite a number of others. It was very pleasing to see nearly all our "stars" turning out and looking really fit. We expected a good race and were not disappointed. As the Brook was in flood, the runners made a lap of the field (nearly a mile) to start, and at the end of this lap it was good to see about 18 runners well bunched together in spite of the fast pace set by Penny, Parker, Taylor and Co. At the half-way mark Penny and Ginty were leading with Parker about 30 yards behind. At this point fifteen runners passed within a minute of the leaders—a very satisfactory state of affairs. The next time we saw the runners was about 400 yards from the finish. A gruelling race was in progress between Penny and Ginty. First one appeared to gain a small advantage, then the other, and they turned into the final straight practically level. Ginty eventually forced himself to the front to win by about seven yards—a splendid race between two very game runners. As the first two finished, Parker entered the finishing straight closely followed by Footer, who had put in some very fast second-half running. The race was a credit to the fitness of all the competitors, and of those making their first attempt, I would particularly mention A. Beaumont. Jim Ginty's Championship win also gave him the handicap, and the improved running of Taylor and R. Patience earned them the minor awards. 1 J. Ginty 58 42 1 45 56 57 1 2 A. W. items.h: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES CHAMPIONSHIP.
items.sum: Report of the South of the Thames Championship at Horsham, where Belgrave's young team, weakened by the eligibility rules, finished 11th; with result and team placings.
items.s: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the South of the Thames Championship at Horsham, where Belgrave's young team, weakened by the eligibility rules, finished 11th; with result and team placings. This Championship was decided this year at Horsham, and as our last year's winning team was no longer eligible, according to the rules govering this event, our chances of being placed were very small. A difficult course and unpleasant weather conditions, still further handicapped our team, which contained several young and comparatively untried runners. In these circumstances, our team position, although lower than our normal performance in this race, must not be regarded with dissatisfaction. In Clements, Lucas, and the younger Herbert, we have three junior runners destined for the highest rank. Beaumont, Wood and Tobin are all likely to show improved performances next year. We detect plenty of evidence of another winning team in a year or two. As in all races where "barring" clauses operate, a club gradually builds up a team year by year until it becomes a winning team. This team in the act of winning (or of being placed in Southern or English Championships) loses its eligibility, and the business of building a new winning team starts all over again! This, of course, is the purpose of the "junior" championships—to encourage the younger and unknown runners. The race result is appended :— m. s. 1 A. J. Hughes (Reading A.C.) 43 12 49 A. F. items.label: June 1937
items.sum: G. S. Doubleday's report of the Southern Cross Country Championships at Horton Kirby, where Belgrave were fifth in the Junior race and the Senior race was abandoned when the trail blew away with Belgrave apparently heading for a big win; Belgrave declined to run in the re-run at Dartford.
items.s: THE SOUTHERN CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. G. S. Doubleday's report of the Southern Cross Country Championships at Horton Kirby, where Belgrave were fifth in the Junior race and the Senior race was abandoned when the trail blew away with Belgrave apparently heading for a big win; Belgrave declined to run in the re-run at Dartford. The venue this time was Horton Kirby, Kent, where a "real" cross-country course had been planned over heavy clay, much of which was "plough" which had been rendered very sticky due to recent rainfall. The "Junior" (5 miles) was held first, and after a fast downhill start the heaviness of the course and the uphill work soon strung the field out. After one small lap (about half-a-mile) Lucas was our first man, lying about 12th, with the rest of the lads coming up. We did not see them again until the finish, where our positions did not seem to have changed, and it was soon obvious that we would not get a place. The winners, Southgate H., finished their four in almost consecutive positions—a fact which brought them applause. That the competitors had had a hard run was obvious by the way in which they trailed up the hill to finish. As for our own team, although many had hoped for a place, it must be remembered that the nature of the course was "foreign" to many of them, and they have nearly all had a strenuous season. Whilst the Juniors were out in the country, the Seniors lined up. Our first disappointment was the absence of Bert Footer and Bert Shaw from the start owing to indisposition. The skies were leaden, a wind was blowing with gale force, and there was blinding rain and hail when the runners left the pens. Fortunately, this storm was short-lived and we were able to see the runners at the end of the short lap. The "Bels" obviously meant business for Pat Parker and Jim Ginty were right at the front, our others being well up, too. As it was a two-lap course we did not see them again until the half-way mark (5 miles), where they were getting mixed up with the tail-end of the Juniors. Jim and Pat had a good 30 yards lead on a Reading man, but lost a few yards lookng for the trail. Both our men looked fresh and comfortable. In the fourth position was Dan Patience, who, running with great power, was overhauling the third man. Our next man was Tom Carter, who, despite the mud, was running with his usual polished style in tenth position. Close on his heels in twelfth position came Arthur Penny, who looked as though he had something up his sleeve (he was wearing a sweater!). Then Harry Shields at eighteenth completed our six. Harry was certainly "having a go," and a sterling performance from him seemed assured. Then there seemed rather a gap before Alf. Taylor and Ron. Patience came along together. Les Cohen soon followed with Arthur Allum close behind him. Our twelve was completed by our reserve men, Micky Walker and, just to make it a family affair, Alec Patience. Thus at half-way our chances of winning the title from Surrey A.C., not to mention a possible individual winner, appeared very bright and all we could do was to wait until the runners had been out in the country again. Then followed a long suspense. Suddenly the runners were sighted, but in the wrong direction. The funnel was reversed, but again they disappeared. It was soon evident that the trail had been lost. Meanwhile, an observer from round the course had reported that the "Bels" had 6 in 12. Then there was a shout and everybody dashed to a barbed wire fence to see the field come straggling uphill over a cabbage field, running from all directions. It was immediately decided to call the race off. It transpired that the high wind had blown the trail away, but, surely, for a Championship Race, something more definite and not subject to the mercy of the elements as is a paper trail is necessary. Or shall each runner be provided with a map and compass? However, the sad fact remains that the entire field ran about twelve miles over very tough country for nothing; and as for many of the runners the "Southern" is their only 10 miles race. it must have been a very galling reward for their winter's training. No less mortifying was the lot of those clubs who had hoped to have earned a high position in the finishing list. For our own part we feel that Fate has robbed us of what appeared to be a potentially phenomenal win—first two men home, two in the next three position, and the other two scoring men inside the dozen. All of our men had gained ground, including Pat and Jim, who at a short distance from the finish had increased their lead to 100 yards. Our complete team of twelve would have closed in by the time that the 60th man was home—surely a performance of which even the wildest optimist would never have dreamed. In the annals of the sport the event will go down as "Race Postponed," but to those who were there (whilst hoping that a similar fate will never befall a race again), I think that it will go down as a moral victory for the Bels. 22 teams closed in. * * * * * It was decided some days later to re-run the Senior race on Easter Saturday, at Dartford. In view of the strenuous programme facing our men, some having Service and International engagements in addition to the normal fixture list, and the unsuitability of the date, we decided not to compete. Our feelings were shared by most other clubs and eventually only 32 individuals, comprising four teams (as against 33 teams originally entered) competed in the re-run race—a truly farcical state of affairs. It is to be hoped that suitable reference is made in the records as to the conditions, size of field, etc., of the re-run race, as there can be no credit in a success of this kind, and it is only fair that future generations shall be reminded that no serious "Southern" Senior Championship was decided in 1937. 1 Southgate H. 55 pts. 2 Polytechnic H. 69 pts. 3 Blackheath H. 96 pts. 4 Chelmsford A.C. 104 pts. 5 Belgrave H. 105 pts. 6 South London H. 110 pts. items.label: June 1937
items.sum: Report of the English Cross Country Championship at Stratford-on-Avon, where Belgrave (94 pts.) lost to Birchfield (90 pts.) by four points despite Jim Ginty third and Pat Parker fourth, with result and team placings.
items.s: THE ENGLISH CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the English Cross Country Championship at Stratford-on-Avon, where Belgrave (94 pts.) lost to Birchfield (90 pts.) by four points despite Jim Ginty third and Pat Parker fourth, with result and team placings. We travelled to Stratford-on-Avon on March 13th, and despite our high hopes, the date proved an unlucky one for us. Unfortunately, we were denied the services of Arthur Penny and Alf Taylor, both of whom had leg troubles; and Carter was in the throes of a severe cold. Despite these handicaps, our lads were determined to give a good account of themselves, and a course consisting of five laps of muddy going on the local racecourse was the test provided. After the first few yards every competitor was well soaked and generally coated with mud, a state of affairs shared to a lesser degree by the officials and spectators present. At the end of the first lap our boys were prominent, as were also Birchfield and several of the Sutton H. (Northern Champions) runners. Jim Ginty and Pat Parker were with the leading bunch, and Dan Patience and Bert Footer were close behind. The second lap showed us to have a twenty to thirty points lead over our Midland rivals, but on the next lap they managed to reduce our lead slightly. In the main, our runners maintained their positions, but the Birchfield runners gradually moved up, although unable to get on terms with our leading runners. With a lap to go our advantage was a bare two points, and we hurried back to the finishing point to await the arrival of the runners and the decision of one of the closest races ever. Belgrave and Birchfield partisans were greatly excited and could hardly contain themselvs whilst awaiting the approach of the runners. Some went down the course to shout on their respective teams, and neither Belgrave nor Birchfield could be confident about the result. The leading runners appeared and H. D. Clark (York H.) narrowly beat R. V. Draper (Hinckley Technical College) for the individual title, with our Jim Ginty a few yards away, third, and Pat Parker fourth. As the first two runners were individual entrants, our team placings scored 1 and 2—the perfect start. Birchfield countered with 8 and 10, and then came Dan Patience, scoring 11 for us. Birchfield's captain, our old friend, R. R. Sutherland, was 12th, and our captain, Bert Footer, followed him in, 13th. Thus, between us we had seven team positions out of the first thirteen, and with four aside scoring, we led by 27 pts. to Birchfield's 47 pts. (Currie (17th) being their fourth man. Birchfield now completed their team with positions 18 and 25, and our fifth man to finish was Les Cohen, 26th. Where was our sixth man? Mr. Austin, the Birchfield Hon. Secretary, acting as Recorder for his club, stood next to the writer, acting in the same capacity for Belgrave. "If your sixth man is behind 37th position, we win," he said, having quickly totalled the scores. And both of us looked anxiously at the stream of runners passing down the "funnel." There was saw our sixth man, Tom Carter, and still we could not tell which team had won. Tom had battled to the last ounce of his strength and collapsed full-length in the tenacious mud. Officials tried to assist him and take the disc recording his position from him; he would not give it to anyone but his own club-man. Eventually, he recovered sufficiently to be helped towards the recording table, and handed his disc to the writer—No. 41! "We win by four points," said Mr. Austin; "fine race!" And so once again we had to take second place to Birchfield, to whom our heartiest congratulations are proffered. They could not boast our splendid start to their team scoring, but their splendid packing and the way they fought for every point commands our admiration. We sighed for Penny and Taylor at their best in our team, and a Carter running as he did the previous year, cold-free; but all teams have their disappointments and patches of hard luck. Now doubt our Midland rivals are also the victims of misfortune on occasions. Certainly, in scoring 90 points they equalled their score of the previous year, and this is a total we have never yet been able to beat. In fact, our score of this year (94 points) is the best we have ever recorded. When we won the title in 1935, our score was 97. Jim Ginty is the first Belgrave man to have been placed in the "National," and we heartily congratulate him; also Pat Parker on exceptionally fine running. Jim was selected for England, and Pat for Northern Ireland, in the "International" following a week later. So, although we were forced into second place after a grand race, we yet can find plenty of satisfaction. Next year we shall be trying again! Our three runners outside our scoring six, backed up well in 60th, 69th and 82nd places. With nine aside scoring we should have beaten every other team in the race. With 4 or 5 aside scoring we should have done the same thing; but with six aside we lose to Birchfield! Next year must see some revision here! A final word of congratulation to J. C. Smart, who finished 34th, running for his Winter first-claim club[illegible] and a comment on the placings of Southern clubs in the team race. Nine of the first twelve clubs from the South, and we are always told that the North and Midlands have the monopoly! 33 teams started. Act. Pos. Team Pos. m. s. 1 H. D. Clark 60 19 2 R. V. items.s: THE FIVE MILE HANDICAP. W. Ashford's report of the Club five mile road handicap, won outright by Pat Parker with W. E. Lucas winning the handicap, with full result. A slightly smaller field than usual lined the start for the five mile road race held on the warmest day this year so far. From the very start Pat Parker looked the winner and after the first mile he was leading, but followed very closely by Carter, Cohen, Stimpson and Ring, with the rest of the field in hot pursuit. The second mile found Parker still leading, with Carter on his heels, and the rest beginning to spread out more. Over the hills Pat had increased his lead to about forty yards, but Cohen, Footer and Stimpson had closed up on Tom Carter, who was apparently having a bad time. Ultimately, Parker ran out winner by about forty-five yards, while Cohen, Footer and Stimpson passed Carter to finish in that order. There was a very keen fight for the next five places, ten seconds covering the five positions. Congratulations to Ted Stimpson for his fine stylish run, his fourth fastest time giving him second handicap prize; and to W. E. Lucas, who won the handicap in splendid fashion. Finally, condolences to Arthur Penny and Alf Taylor, who generally finish well up in the race but were unfit this year. † Dead Heat. 1 J. Parker 28 48 0 20 28 28 12 2 L. J. items.label: June 1937
items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the London to Brighton Relay, in which Belgrave led from the second to the ninth stage but lost to Mitcham A.C. by a yard, with Birchfield third, followed by the result.
items.s: THE BRIGHTON RELAY. Stage-by-stage report of the London to Brighton Relay, in which Belgrave led from the second to the ninth stage but lost to Mitcham A.C. by a yard, with Birchfield third, followed by the result. This year's Brighton Relay differed greatly from previous races in that a much shorter distance course was used, divided into ten stages as usual. The stages to suffer most were the last three and on these the distances were cut down appreciably. We had hoped to record our fourth successive win, but in most dramatic finish ever seen, we lost on the last stage by a bare yard. Congratulations to Mitcham A.C. upon providing such a sensational "turn-up." The start was from the "News of the World" Track at Mitcham. We lacked the services once again of Art Penny and A. E. Taylor, and, most unfortunately, Jim Ginty was also unable to help our team. Bert Footer was our first runner. During the preceding week he had told us the usual tales of being off-colour, unfit and unworthy of a place in the team. As usual, we had discounted his statement (to put it mildly!) but on this occasion he was certainly not quite his usual self. Probably missed Dale Hill, but anyway at the end of the first stage we were in ninth position of the 21 competing clubs. Mitcham led from Birchfield and Reading at this point. Pat Parker, our next runner, followed with one of the most sensational runs ever seen in this race. With tremendous stride, amazing power, intense determination and relentless pace, he passed the eight runners who started before him, and took us into the lead. Previous record over this stretch was hopelessly smashed! If this run had been accomplished on the track in front of a large crowd, it would have been hailed as one of the classic efforts to be spoken of with hushed voice in years to come. As it is, witnessed by the few, it will long remain an outstanding memory to those privileged to be present whilst Pat turned a deficit into a nine seconds lead. Les Cohen now carried our colours from Merstham to Earlswood Common. The lead was increased to one of 25 seconds over Birchfield, with Mitcham still in the third place. Cohen's effort was a very fine one, and we now seemed well set for our fourth victory. A. R. Shaw followed for us. Bert not only maintained our lead but added a few yards to it. Birchfield were second, Mitcham third and Achilles fourth at the end of this, the fourth, stage. Syd Ring was the next entrusted with the baton, and at the end of his stage it was still in our possession. Owing to a misunderstanding, the change-over was made on the lower road instead of on the higher path outside "The Half Moon Hotel." Accordingly, the times issued can only be regarded as approximate, and certainly not accurate for the stage. Ring certainly had more than a two-seconds lead over the Mitcham runner who had taken second place from Birchfield. William Lucas, our reserve runner, still a junior, now took over. Owing to the inability of Ginty to run at the last moment, Lucas was brought into the team and ran with conspicuous success. With a veteran's knowledge of pace, and in style indicative of a coming champion, he pursued his way, and at the Handcross change-over point we had 18 seconds over Mitcham and 20 seconds over Birchfield. Tom Carter was our seventh runner and he set about consolidating our positon with a will. Over the longest stage of the race, over six miles, he gave of his best and our advantage over the second team was increased to 46 seconds. Birchfield had now recovered second position. Harry Shields, Captain, now took his turn, and in typical fashion put all his energy into his running, with such good effect that the lead was increased to one of 50 seconds. The eighth stage finished and victory seemed to be in sight. Ted Stimpson carried on in steady, long striding style, running easily. Meantime, Birchfield and Mitcham were fighting each other, and in doing so gained on our runner. Stimpson, still running easily, yet seemed unable to increase his pace, and Biggs (Birchfield) and Jones (Mitcham), English and Welsh Internationals respectively, continued to gain. At the end of the stage we still led, but our margin was much reduced. Arthur Allum was our last representative. He had nine seconds lead from Birchfield and eleven seconds from Mitcham. Could he hold this over the last 3 6/10 miles? We knew that there would only be a few yards in it at the finish, but which runner would break the tape? Feverishly our bus and coach, loaded with Club supporters, made for Brighton after stopping to give our man a cheer. But try as we could, we were unable to get through the traffic and reach the finishing point before the runners. Heads bobbed about in front of us, and Belgrave still led at the Aquarium, with only the few yards along the Front remaining. Inches only divided the leading runners, however, and in the last few yards the Mitcham runners made a supreme effort, and they had won by a yard. Allum, game to the last stride, was disappointed, but had not spared himself and ran well. Birchfield followed 12 seconds behind, so Arthur actually increased his lead over our Midland rivals. Mitcham A.C. were naturally elated at their win, which came as a surprise to all, including even themselves. The enlistment of many Welch Internationals, now employed at Tooting Bec Mental Hospital, plus the A.A.A. "Hard Cases" Sub-committee, which has power to suspend the operation of the normal qualifying period in special cases, has done much to strengthen the Mitcham team in the past few months. Among these new recruits are some very fine runners, and it will be interesting to see if Mitcham can maintain the high position they have now earned for themselves. We had the satisfaction of beating Birchfield again, so compensating in some measure for our "National" defeat. This, too, without Penny and Ginty in our team! Fourth came Surrey A.C. and fifth, Achilles, who had been freely mentioned as possible winners. Our team and supporters had the usual happy journey homewards, and so finished yet another day of sport on the Brighton Road, to be added to our store of memories. RESULT. items.s: ROUND THE TRACKS. Preview of Belgrave's Jubilee track season fixtures for June to August 1937, with club handicaps, championship standards and entry details from the Asst. Hon. Sec. We are now getting into our strides in this, our Jubilee Track season, and so far the results have augured well for the future. By the time you read this we shall have had two of the Inter-Club Relay Contests, and the County Championships will have come and gone. Our first meeting at Battersea Park will be on June 9th, and we trust the new dressing rooms will be ready for use by then. We have a triangular match with the Essex Relay and Team champions, Leigh-on-Sea H., and the Imperial College A.C., who can call on some more than useful performers. Club Handicaps on this evening will be: 100 yards, 880 yards, 100 yards (under 19), Long Jump and 2 Miles Walk. We are also holding the Club 3 Miles Track Championship for the "Griffin" Cup, (holder, A. W. Penny). On recent form it looks as though a new holder will be found! There will be two races open to all Unattached Novices, viz., 100 yards x 1 mile run. Entry is free, so please tell any of your friends who are willing to see what athletic ability they possess. On June 12th, at the Civil Service Meeting on the White City track, will be held the S.A.A.L. 1 Mile Team race, and I hope we shall gain much-needed points in this event. Then, for June 16th we have the S.A.A.L. 3 Miles Team race at the Herne Hill track. This is a distance at which our boys always show up well, and we should gain maximum points here. The following evening, June 17th, we are at Richmond on the palatial athletic ground, for the "Doris" Shield contest with Thames Valley Harriers, who are joint holders of the Shield with ourselves. The other participants will be the Ashcombe St. George's A.C., who should prove a stronger force now that they have amalgamated. There will be the usual Handicaps open to all Club members: 100 yards, 1 Mile run, 2 Miles Walk. Just drop me a card if you wish to enter, and I trust our members will support this very old-established meeting. It is essential that definite entries at an early date are received from members for this meeting, as the handicap allowances are decided by a Joint Committee of the three Clubs. On Saturday, June 19th, at the new track in Ladywell Recreation Ground, will be held the Southern Junior Championships. Any members who are under 19 years of age and would like to enter should get in touch with H. M. Quackenbos, our Junior Captain. On June 23rd we have the third Inter-Club Relay contest, this time at Epsom, and I trust we shall get the same support here as we do when nearer home. On Saturday, June 26th, the Southern Senior Championships will be held at Preston Park, near Brighton. A cheap return fare of 6/5 has been arranged for trains as follows: Victoria 1 p.m., London Bridge 1-5 p.m.; arrive Brighton at 2 p.m. We come then to Club Championship Day, July 3rd, at Battersea Park Track. There will be the usual Championships, although this year we are also giving standard medals for the 220 yards Senior race. Other standards are: 440 yards, 56 secs.; 880 yards, 2 min. 8 secs.; 1 Mile, 4 min. 50 secs. Also for the Field Events Championships, standards have been fixed, so I hope members will enter and so show your Committee that their efforts on the members' behalf are at least appreciated. There will be the usual Boys (under 15), 100 yards Championship, and with S.R. Gardner no longer eligible, a new holder will have to be found. A new 100 yards (under 19) race has been arranged in addition to the old 220 yards which is, this year, also for those under 19. Another innovation is the 880 yards (under 19) Championship, so I think everyone will agree that our Juniors are being well catered for. We do not favour "Victor Ludorum" contests, so hope our Juniors will select the event they are best suited for and enter accordingly. This is our Jubilee Championship Meeting. We are holding more events than ever before, and therefore I look to the entries being the largest ever. Don't forget Saturday,, July 3rd, and please let me have your name in good time for programme purposes. On July 10th, the A.A.A. Junior Championships will be held at the White City and here again the advice of our Junior Captain should be sought. On July 14th, at Battersea Park, we have a Junior match with Thames Valley Harriers, and in addition, the following Club Handicaps: 100 yards (under 16), 100 yards (Vets. over 40), 220 yards, 880 yards, 2 Miles Run, 2 Miles Walk and Javelin. There will also be a 1 Mile Walk open to all unattached Novices. We come then to the A.A.A. General Championships which are held on Friday evening, July 16th, and Saturday, July 17th. On the form shewn in our own Championships will depend the Club entrants, and I am sure that our representatives will do us full justice. We have then two Inter-Club matches, one with the London Transport (Central Buses) which will be at the new Tooting Track on July 19th; and then on July 22nd we have a return Junior match with Thames Valley Harriers at Richmond. On July 28th, at the "News of the World" Track, Mitcham, will be the final Inter-Club Relay contest, and I hope by then we shall be well ahead on points. At Battersea Park on July 31st, we meet old friends in the London Athletic Club. They have some very famous runners in their ranks—J. V. Powell, A. W. Sweeney, B. F. McCabe, to mention just a few, and we look forward to providing them with worthy opposition. There will also be Club Handicaps as follows: 220 yards, 880 yards, 2 Miles Run, 880 yards (under 19), Shot Putt and 2 Miles Walk. The season by now will be well under way, and we then have our usual August evening meeting, on the 11th, at Battersea Park. Club Handicaps will be: 100 yards, 440 yards, 1 Mile, Long Jump and 2 Miles Walk. There then remains but two fixtures on our card, but I will write of these in our next issue. I hope you will make a note of the above dates. Any further information will gladly be given and early entries will be much appreciated. All entries and enquiries to E. A. Duffett, Asst. Hon. items.label: June 1937
items.h: MATCH AT DRAYTON GREEN TRACK, May 8th.
items.sum: W. E. Lucas reports a four-club track match at Drayton Green won by Belgrave with 35 points from Reading A.C., Ealing H. and Ashcombe-St. George's.
items.s: MATCH AT DRAYTON GREEN TRACK, May 8th. W. E. Lucas reports a four-club track match at Drayton Green won by Belgrave with 35 points from Reading A.C., Ealing H. and Ashcombe-St. George's. Four clubs took part in this match, namely, Ashcombe-St. Georg'es, Reading A.C., Ealing H. and ourselves. We started rather badly, as our sprinters were unable to gain a place in the 100 yards final. This deficit, however, was soon overcome, for we gained the first three places in the 1 Mile, led by Pat Parker. In the 880 yards which followed, Alby Bird showed fine form in gaining first place with Frank Webb also scoring. Again in the 220 yards our sprinters were unable to make any headway, but this was again nullified as our boys, Tom Carter, Arthur Allum and Tommy Morrell, ran well to win the 2 Miles. The 1 Mile Medley Relay proved the high spot of the afternoon for a battle ensued throughout which was not decided until the last few yards. It ended in a win for Ealing H., with Reading and ourselves neck and neck for second place. The Reading boy, however, just managed to hold off Les Bennett, who ran well over the last 220 yards. The final result was: Belgrave H. 35 pts., Reading A.C. 31 pts., Ealing H. 23 pts., Ashcombe-St. George's 13 pts. Thus we made a good start to what we hope will be a very successful track season. W. items.label: August 1937
items.sum: Editorial notes on the club's bronze medals in the A.A.A. 4 x 440 yards relay, members' A.A.A. Championship placings, a Sporting Life club points table, joint Waddilove Trophy win at Birmingham, junior promise, poor S.A.A.L. form, a wedding and the coming London–Brighton walk.
items.s: Editorial notes on the club's bronze medals in the A.A.A. 4 x 440 yards relay, members' A.A.A. Championship placings, a Sporting Life club points table, joint Waddilove Trophy win at Birmingham, junior promise, poor S.A.A.L. form, a wedding and the coming London–Brighton walk. Heartiest congratulations to our team placed third in the Amateur Athletic Association's 4 x 440 yards Relay Championship. This is the first time we have ever been placed, and Messrs. Pack, Michael, Herbert and Bird will value their bronze medals. Our team ran impressively in their heat, and in the final Eddie Pack gave our team a splendid start, unofficial watches timing him to do a shade outside 50 seconds. Dick Michael then took over, and striding magnificently, retained the lead, although our opponents were gaining. L. W. Herbert took the next "leg" for us and despite a plucky effort was passed by J. V. Powell (L.A.C.) the International runner; and the Achilles runner. Alby Bird was our last man, and he could not be expected to give Halford (L.A.C.) and Barnes (Achilles) a start. Bird held his position, however, and was content to ease off in the finishing straight when third place was secure (South London H. were fourth) and first and second teams could not be overtaken. Our team and all Belgrave Harriers present were delighted. Not only was it an historical moment for the Club, but it shows that we are within measurable distance of an A.A.A. Relay title. A little more improvement and our track teams may well command the respect during the Summer, that our teams are accorded in the Winter months. * * * * * In the A.A.A. Championships proper, a week later, our representatives acquitted themselves well. Pat Parker was placed third in the 3 miles race (his time being 14 min. 28 sec.), and earned selection against France the following week. Don Brown was third and Percy Wright fourth in the 2 miles walk, and Eddie Pack finished fourth in the final of the 440 yards championship. His time was 49 1-5 sec. and he is the fastest quarter-mile we have had since the days of George Dunckley. In fact, Eddie's running would have gained him a title in some years. We were also glad to see J. Dodd, representing the Northern Counties A.A., win the Pole Vault. Dodd hopes to be back again with us shortly, following on his studies in the North, and we shall have a welcome for him. Club members to gain standard medals, additional to those previously mentioned, were A. A. Bird (880 yards), A. W. Penny (6 miles), L. Cohen (3 miles), A. R. Shaw (Steeplechase), F. A. Walker and A. F. Mitchell (Marathon). * * * * * It may be remembered that two years ago we suggested that a trophy might be awarded to the club whose first-claim representatives scored most points, reckoning on six points for a winner downwards, and a point for every standard gained. No official notice has ever been taken of the idea, but it was interesting to see that this year the "Sporting Life" compiled a table giving winners six points down to one point for sixth place. This table took into consideration the distance championships decided earler in the year, and was as follows :— This shows us in a deservedly favourable position, and if E. H. Pack and J. Dodd had appeared on the programme in the club name, our tally would have been even more impressive. * * * * * On July 24th we sent a team to Birmingham to compete in the "Waddilove" Trophy track competition for the first time. Birchfield Harriers have been anxious for years that we should participate, and at our first attempt we were glad to become joint-holders with the London A.C. of the handsome trophy. We were successful in winning the Two Miles team race through the efforts of A. W. Penny, L. J. Cohen and E. S. Stimpson; and took second place in the Relay (won by Birchfield), our team being A. A. Bird, R. G. Michael, S. C. Botwright and E. Gray. In addition Bird ran wonderfully well to finish second to J. V. Powell, beaten by a yard and a half in 1 min. 57 3-5 seconds. E. Gray was placed third in the 100 yards. Final scores were : Belgrave H. and L.A.C., 12 points each; Birchfield H., 10 pts.; the holders, Achilles, scoring 1 point only. All our runners did well, and we returned feeling well satisfied with our first visit to Perry Bar. Several of our Junior runners, too, have taken the eye and promise well for the future. Our relay team in the 4 x 110 yards Junior A.A.A. Championship qualified for the final and finished close up fourth. B. Saunders and F. Skelley showed up well. Skelley has, of course, earned our congratulations by virtue of winning the Southern Junior Long Jump Championship, and in taking second place in the A.A.A. Junior Championship with a fine leap of 21ft. 6½in. Several others in our colours showed good style and may be expected to be in the top class when physical maturity arrives. We have had much pleasure in welcoming so many promising junior runners during the Summer season, and if their interest continues, as we have no doubt it will, our future on the track looks very bright. * * * * * It is curious that we should have had such a poor season in Southern Amateur Athletic League track events, when otherwise we have enjoyed much success. For example, we finished last in the S.A.A.L. 4 x 440 yards race (the Club Outing the day before may, perhaps, be blamed!) and yet practically the same team took third place in the A.A.A. Championship! Strange, yet, true! Our comparatively poor form in S.A.A.L. events gives us added interest in the final event of this competition, the One Mile Medley Race, on August 21st. On this result depends whether we continue in Division I, in which we have competed since its inception, or whether we are relegated to Division II next season. Whichever way things go, we may be sure that we shall give these fixtures greater attention next season. If we continue in the upper ranks we shall be out to make sure that our position is not endangered, as has happened this year. If we compete in Division II it will be our earnest endeavour to head the League and regain our lost place. Certainly, this year's poor showing should shock us into doing something better next season. * * * * * Congratulations and best wishes to J. C. Edwards, who was recently taken unto himself a wife. Best of luck! * * * * * On September 4th the London—Brighton Walk takes place, starting from Westminster at 7 a.m. We shall have several entrants and as usual the Club Long Distance Championship, which carries with it the "Belgrave Cup," will take place in conjunction with the main race. We shall have a bus on the road, leaving Big Ben at 7-30 a.m., and anyone desiring a seat (5/- fare) is asked to communicate with the Walking Hon. Secretary at once. This is always a good day out, and we hope to have a number of supporters on the road. Anyone willing to act as cyclist attendant to our walkers is asked to get in touch with the Walking Hon. Secretary. * * * * * The Club year is approaching its end, and late in September, on a date to be advised, the Annual General Meeting will take place. It is the duty of all members to attend if they can possibly do so, and ensure that a representative and hard-working set of officials and committee are elected to guide the fortunes of the Club in the ensuing season. This is your responsibility. See that you attend the A.G.M. and carry out the privileges and obligations of membership in full. * * * * * Congratulations to A. A. Bird, L. J. Cohen and P. G. Wright, who have by virtue of gaining A.A.A. items.label: August 1937
items.sum: Round-up of members' performances at the Kinnaird Competition, Southern Counties steeplechase and marathon, county and Southern championships and open meetings in 1937.
items.s: ROUND THE MEETINGS. Round-up of members' performances at the Kinnaird Competition, Southern Counties steeplechase and marathon, county and Southern championships and open meetings in 1937. In the "Kinnaird" Competition, held on May 29th, we failed to gain a point and yet there were several very fine performances by our members. It is to be hoped that one year we shall really be in a position to make a determined effort to wrest the "Kinaird" Trophy from its usual holders, Achilles Club. We have always felt that the system of scoring, and the events comprising the competition, hardly favour us, and we should dearly like to see a competition which included the other events held at the meeting, viz., Steeplechase, Marathon and Team Walk, and the addition of, say, the Javelin Throw. The choice of events is, of course, a matter for the promoters, the Polytechnic Harriers, whose kind invitation to participate we are always glad to accept. In the "non-Kinnaird" events we did well. Our walkers dead-heated for first place with Woodford Green A.C. In the Southern Counties Steeplechase Championship, we had second and third men to finish in C. T. Carter and A. R. Shaw. The Marathon was run under tropical conditions and only seven men finished inside standard time. The remainder of the competitors were not permitted to finish on the track owing to the Stadium authorities' restrictions. We were the only club to finish three men (Messrs. A. F. Mitchell, F. A. Walker and F. G. White) and at a committee meeting of the Polytechnic Harriers, the special carved oak team awards were voted to our men. We congratulate them upon finishing the course on an extremely difficult day. In the County Championships, some of our men were seen to advantage. E. H. Pack won the Middlesex 440 yards championship, and A. A. Bird was third in the 880 yards, and T. D. Wiley third in the 440 yards Hurdles at the same meeting. Percy Wright distinguished himself by taking second place in the Walk, returning excellent time. He has since been invited to represent Middlesex. In the Surrey championships, Don Brown and Joe Coleman were first and third in the Walk; and L. W. Herbert was narrowly beaten in the 880 yards race. When Herbert has learned to run his first 300 yards a little faster and in company, we shall expect him to beat 1 min. 56 sec. for half-mile. In the Southern Championships held at Brighton, Brown was second to Cooper in the 2 miles Walk, and Bird finished fourth in the 880 yards, inside A.A.A. standard time. At the various Open meetings, several of our men have been prominent, notably T. D. Wiley and S. C. Botwright, who have not been content with single wins! Congratulations to all who have caught the judge's eye! Restrictions of space do not permit a full list of successes, and have also prevented the publication of an article by T. F. items.label: August 1937
items.sum: Report of the Coronation team and relay meeting at Broomfield Park, Southgate, on 15 May 1937, where Belgrave finished third behind Southgate and Blackheath, with handicap wins for Belgrave.
items.s: THE CORONATION MEETING AT SOUTHGATE. Report of the Coronation team and relay meeting at Broomfield Park, Southgate, on 15 May 1937, where Belgrave finished third behind Southgate and Blackheath, with handicap wins for Belgrave. On May 15th, at Broomfield Park, the local club, Southgate Harriers, entertained Blackheath H., Polytechnic H. and ourselves in a series of team and relay events. Also on the programme were handicaps open to members of the four competing clubs. We were more or less outclassed in the sprint events, Blackheath winning both the 4 x 110, and 4 x 220 yards. Also, owing to the earliness of the season, we could not field a team for the 4 x 440 yards. The 4 x 880 yards was held in conjunction with the Southern Amateur League event at this distance, and although L. W. Herbert gave us the lead over the first stage, we eventually finished in fourth place, beating Mitcham A.C. and Herne Hill H. Southgate pleased the local crowd by just beating the Poly after a very close and exciting race. In the 1 Mile Team Race, Pat Parker strode round in the lead, only to be beaten up the straight by P. E. Bull, of the Poly H. When the points had been added up it was found that Blackheath and Belgrave each scored 29, with Polytechnic 38, and Southgate 40. We also fielded a team in the 1 Mile relay open to those who had not competed before that afternoon in the match events—in other words, a reserves race—but an unfortunate blunder at the first take-over resulted in the baton being dropped and so put our team out of the race. So far, during the afternoon we had not gained many points, but along came our field event men to show the runners how it should be done! We won the Weight Putt with Grassau and Melchior, also the Javelin with George Powell and, once again, Melchior, who, by the way, materially contributed to our total of points. The result of the match was : Southgate H., 37 pts.; Blackheath H., 34½ pts.; Belgrave H., 25½ pts.; Polytechnic H., 24 pts. Our runners were more to the fore in the handicap events; mainly due to the fact that we provided the larger portion of the entries, especially in the 880 yards, which was won by Alby Bird off 8 yards. He ran splendidly to beat W. E. Lucas on the tape, so that Belgrave had the first two home. The souvenir awards which were presented to all winners and runners-up were much appreciated by the competitors, and our best thanks are due to the Southgate Harriers for promoting such an interesting and pleasant afternoon's sport. items.label: August 1937
items.h: MATCH versus OLD TIFFINIANS A.C. AND OLD MID-WHITGIFTIANS.
items.sum: Report of the evening match at Kingston on 27 May 1937 against Old Tiffinians A.C. and Old Mid-Whitgiftians, in which Belgrave were second.
items.s: MATCH versus OLD TIFFINIANS A.C. AND OLD MID-WHITGIFTIANS. Report of the evening match at Kingston on 27 May 1937 against Old Tiffinians A.C. and Old Mid-Whitgiftians, in which Belgrave were second. We were again blessed with a fine evening on May 27th for our match at Kingston. A very good and keenly contested meeting resulted which was very much appreciated by the spectators. I am sure, however, that the high-lights of the meeting were our Shot Putters. Grassau, Jones and Bill Sutton monopolised the crowd once they started, and apparently they had not met men of their magnificent physique before. Points were secured for us by E. L. Kealey (3rd, 100 yards); T. D. Wiley (3rd, 220 yards); A. H. Sampson (3rd, 440 yards); S. Garland and W. Ashford (2nd and 3rd, 880 yards); A. A. Bird and E. Stimpson (2nd and 3rd, 1 mile); E. L. Blyther (3rd, Long Jump); T. D. Wiley (1st, High Jump); F. Grassau and S. Jones (1st and 2nd, Shot Putt). The Relay was won by our hosts, with our team second; and final scores were : Old Tiffinians, 44 pts.; Belgrave H., 28 pts.; Old Mid-Whitgiftians, 9 points. Thus concluded another most enjoyable fixture at the Old Tiffiinian's hospitable headquarters. Grassau Grassau Jones Jones Bill Sutton Bill Sutton shot putter E. L. Kealey E. L. items.h: THE INTER-CLUB RELAYS AT TOOTING TRACK.
items.sum: Report of the first Inter-Club Relay Shield contest of the season at the new Tooting Track, with club handicaps run at the same meeting.
items.s: THE INTER-CLUB RELAYS AT TOOTING TRACK. Report of the first Inter-Club Relay Shield contest of the season at the new Tooting Track, with club handicaps run at the same meeting. The first of the contests for the Inter-Club Relay Shield was held at the new Tooting Track. It was also the first time that one of these contests had been held on a Saturday, the usual practise being to run them on week-nights. From our point of view, however, the change was quite a success, although the track was on the loose side. Given time, we are sure this pleasantly situated ground will prove popular with the South London athletes. In the first event, the 4 x 100 yards, we fielded quite a useful team; and, with F. W. Pritchard running a fine third leg, we had the satisfaction of beating Mitcham A.C., with Epsom beating Croydon for third place. The 4 x 880 yards saw Dick Michael give us the lead on the first stage, but F. H. C. White was caught and passed by the Mitcham runner. Alby Bird went next and, running with fine judgment, soon overhauled his man, and sent L. W. Herbert off with a useful lead. Herbert ran well within himself and kept off the opposition without much trouble. Epsom again beat Croydon for third place; and their half-milers are beginning to weld themselves into a useful team. We welcomed Eddie Kealey back into the active ranks for this meeting; while S. C. Botwright also turned out for us in the 4 x 300 yards. Tom Wiley went first and gave us the lead, which F. W. Pritchard and Botwright kept, to send Kealey away with a winning margin. Croydon reversed their placings with Epsom in this event. Then came the 1 Mile Team race, and although we were without Pat Parker and Les Cohen, our team, led home by W. E. Lucas, ran well to win the team race. Harry Shields caused quite a stir by dashing into the lead when 300 yards from home and this seemed to act as a winning tonic to our team. We had a few club handicaps at this meeting and in the 220 yards for Juniors, under 19, F. J. Skelley showed he was in sprinting form by winning from the 5 yards mark. G. H. Knight, a newcomer to our ranks, gave him a close race off 15 yards, and the scratch man, B. Saunders, ran well to gain third place. In the 2 Miles Walk, E. C. A. Heather made a welcome reappearance and, with the handicapper being kind to him, won off 475 yards, with another long-marker in W. G. True, off 650 yards, second. Joe Coleman walked with plenty of strength and determination to finish third. The 880 yards handicap was interesting because of the fine effort made by L. W. Herbert, off 25 yards. He cut through the field on the second lap, and won in fine style, with E. J. Selby (75) second, and S. Garland, off 45 yards, third. Our first field event handicap of the season was the Shot Putt and E. L. Blyther (13ft. 6in.) showed improvement over previous performances by taking first place with 38ft. 8in. R. E. Stride, Snr. (16ft. 0in.) was second with 37ft. 4in. and S. Jones (1ft. 0in.) did well with 37ft. 0in. to take third place. F. W. Pritchard F. W. items.label: August 1937
items.sum: Review of Belgrave's 1937 season in Division I of the Southern Amateur Athletic League: the 4 x 880 yards, 4 x 220 yards, 1 mile and 3 miles team races, the 4 x 440 yards relay, the coming medley relay and the field events section.
items.s: THE SOUTHERN ATHLETIC LEAGUE. Review of Belgrave's 1937 season in Division I of the Southern Amateur Athletic League: the 4 x 880 yards, 4 x 220 yards, 1 mile and 3 miles team races, the 4 x 440 yards relay, the coming medley relay and the field events section. As already mentioned elsewhere in this issue, the first of the contests in the S.A.A.L., Division I, was the 4 x 880 yards held at Southgate, on May 15th. Owing to the earliness of the season, our team was not at full strength and some of the other competing clubs were in a similar position. Southgate made an excellent debut in the 1st Division by beating the Poly in a close race. The other placings were : Blackheath 3, Belgrave 4, Mitcham 5, and Herne Hill H. 6. The next event was the 4 x 220 yards at the "Kinnard" meeting at the White City. Sprinters have never been our strong point, and we were not very optimistic about our chances here. As expected, Blackheath were winners, with Herne Hill H. second, and the Poly third. Then came Southgate H., and we just managed to beat our rivals, Mitcham A.C., for last place. So far, results had not been too encouraging, but with the longer distances to come we were confident that we would be more to the fore. The 1 Mile team race was held at the White City in conjunction with the Civil Service meeting, and without doubt was the finest event on the programme. Pat Parker soon went to the front and led the field round at a good pace. Out team were running well, and the biggest danger appeared to be Blackheath. Over the last lap Hodges, of Southgate, went in front, followed by Poole, Blackheath, and A. V. Reeve, of the Poly. Pat had dropped to fifth place but by a determined effort down the straight he pegged one back and so finished 4th. W. E. Lucas had run well to gain 8th place, and Tom Carter and Ted Stimpson finished in 12th and 13th positions. We had to wait until the judges had sorted the men out and then came the result : Polytechnic H. 35 pts., Blackheath H 36 pts., Belgrave H. 37 pts. Thus we had lost first place by two points, and yet were placed only third. A closer finish could not be imagined and although scoring one point less than last year, when we were second, we were now one place worse off! We came then to the 3 Miles team race, which was held at the Herne Hill Track. In the individual race, D. B. Pell, of Herne Hill H., ran a fine race to win from Hodges, of Southgate, with Les Cohen, of our own club, third. We seem always to be the unlucky club when it comes to close finishes in team races; and this was no exception. When the points had been totalled up it was found that Mitcham A.C. scored 31, with Belgrave 32. Of the other members of our team, Tom Carter was 6th, with Arthur Penny 7th, while Harry Shields had an off day in being placed 16th. Thus, if Pat Parker had been there it would have been "in the bag," but I seem to remember other occasions when we have had cause to think of the old saying, "there's many a slip . . . . " The 4 x 440 yards was held on a Monday evening at the new Ladywell Park track. While not being the best of days on which to hold a sports meeting, the track was also in a very loose state, and the running of the meeting left much to be desired. As to the race itself, Polytechnic H. were the winners from Southgate H., with Herne Hill H. 3rd, Blackheath 4th, Mitcham A.C. 5th, and the "Bels" last. It must be said in fairness to our lads that on the previous day they had been on the Club's outing to Littlehampton and their strenuous exertions "by the sea" had not left them in a very fit state for running. The irony of the thing is that a week later the same team, with Eddie Park, taking the place of Tom Scrimshaw, gained third place in the A.A.A. 4 x 440 yards relay! The last event in the League programme is the 1 Mile Medley Relay on August 21st, at Herne Hill. We have not been able to ascertain the correct league placings, but are informed that we lead Herne Hill H. and Mitcham A.C. by 1 point for last place. As the bottom club is relegated to the 2nd Division, it looks as if there is every possibility of the "Bels" being the unlucky one. However, the race had not been run yet, so here's hoping! Whatever the result, I am sure our boys will enter upon next season's contests with just the same enthusiasm they have shewn during the present one, which after all is the spirit we want. The results can look after themselves. As regards the Field Events Section of the League, I understand we are at present leading in this contest, but here again we have been unable to find out the positions in the table. It seems as though this season has not shewn quite the same success as in the past. By this I mean among the clubs generally; and it looks very much as if the whole position will have to be overhauled at the next A.G.M. of the S.A.A.L. items.s: INTER-CLUB RELAYS AT CROYDON. Report of the second Inter-Club relay contest at the Croydon Harriers' ground on June 1st (4 x 100, 4 x 880, 4 x 300 yards and mile team race), leaving Belgrave leading Mitcham on points. The second Inter-Club relay contest was held on June 1st at the Croydon Harriers' ground. Mitcham appeared to have a stronger team and seemed out to prevent a repetition of the Tooting result. In the 4 x 100 yards Mitcham were first with ourselves just beating Croydon for second place. The 4 x 880 yards saw a ding-dong battle between the "Mental Hospital" boys and our lads; and over the first leg Frank Webb was just beaten by Leadbeater. P. Dee, the Welsh "crack," went next, with Alby Bird in hot pursuit. The leader, however, was not to be caught and, running in strong style, increased his club's lead. Our Track Captain, Harry Shields, not only caught his rival, but sent L. W. Herbert off with a slight lead. Roberts, the young Mitcham runner, trailed his man well, but nearing home Herbert went away to win in convincing fashion. Our team in the 4 x 300 yards started off well, F. W. Pritchard giving us the lead which Botwright kept. We then ran G. Camkin, who was making his first appearance in these contests, but although he tried hard enough, Mitcham, and then Croydon, passed him. Tom Wiley was thus given a hopeless task in attempting to catch the leader, but running in determined style, he beat the Croydon runner down the straight to give us second place. We came then to the Mile team race and, after a good race, Mitcham beat us by two points. They had the first two home in Dee and Brickwood; and although our boys finished 4, 5, 6, 7, it was not good enough! Thus at the end of the evening the points up to date were: Belgrave H., 29; Mitcham A.C., 27; Epsom H., 12; Croydon H., 12. items.sum: Report of the club meeting on June 9th: a triangular match with Imperial College A.C. and Leigh-on-Sea Harriers, the Club 3 Miles Championship won by Les Cohen, club handicaps, a walk handicap and a novices' mile.
items.s: CLUB MEETING ON JUNE 9th. Report of the club meeting on June 9th: a triangular match with Imperial College A.C. and Leigh-on-Sea Harriers, the Club 3 Miles Championship won by Les Cohen, club handicaps, a walk handicap and a novices' mile. On this evening we had a triangular match with Imperial College A.C. and the Leigh-on-Sea Harriers. The Club 3 Miles Championship was also decided, and in addition we had two races open to unattached novices on the programme. Tom Wiley won the 100 yards match, with F. W. Pritchard third. An Imperial College man was second, with Leigh gaining fourth place. We also had first two home in the 220 yards, S. C. Botwright and F. W. Pritchard doing the needful. Pat Parker turned out for us in the Mile and won in easy fashion, with A. R. Shaw second. Towell, of Leigh, was third, with Britton, Imperial College, fourth. Eddie Pack was also a starter in the 440 yards match, but was content to take things easy after his Middlesex County win the previous Saturday. Alby Bird raced into the lead, with Pack following, and they finished in that order, with Leigh filling third and fourth places. We thus led easily on the track events, but some closer competition was seen in the field contests. F. Grassau did 37ft. 8½in. in the Shot Putt, and C. A. Melchior gained third place with 31ft. 4in. The High Jump saw Leigh and the Imperial College gaining the points; and in the Javelin, M. Bradley threw 147ft. 9in., to beat Melchior. T. C. Jones won the Long Jump match; and also proved the winner of the club Long Jump handicap. The 3 Miles club championship saw a field of 14, although Pat Parker decided not to compete. He rather wisely preferred to concentrate on the shorter distances until later in the season, and his running in the recent A.A.A. championships proved the wisdom of his decision. Ted Stimpson cut out the pace in the early stages, but a little bunch of runners soon moved up to him, and then J. C. Smart had bad luck in sustaining a fall which put him out of the race. We then saw Les Cohen, Tom Carter, and Arthur Penny move away from the rest; although Dan Patience was running well close behind. In the last lap a hectic struggle ensued. The pace proved too much for Penny, and down the straight Cohen got the better of Carter in a rousing finish. Dan Patience also sprinted past Arthur Penny near the tape, although it seemed as if the latter had thrown his hand in. 1st class standards were gained by A. W. Penny, A. H. Sampson (who ran very well over this distance), H. W. Shields and Arthur Allum. 2nd class medals were also gained by Alf Taylor and R. W. Tobin. In the club handicaps we saw F. J. Skelley run well to gain second place in the 100 yards, under 19. G. K. Talbot, with 7 yards start, proved the winner. Skelley was off 1 yard, and L. F. Barber, off 6 yards, was third. A newcomer in A. S. Blunden won the club 100 yards, off 8½ yards, with S. C. Botwright, off 7 yards (a mark he will not see again), second, and Alec Mewes, with 5½ yards, third. The latter certainly seems to run better in club handicaps than he does in open competition, but perhaps he is saving it up. Who knows? As was generally expected, W. E. Lucas took advantage of his mark to win the 880 yards in fast time. J. H. Chantler ran well to gain second place, with Tommy Morrell third. Apart from the winner, the finish was very close, a bunch of runners making a dash at the finishing line. In the 2 Miles Walk handicap, L. J. Coleman made good use of his mark; with another long marker in W. G. True, second. Charlie Redgrave made a welcome re-appearance and walked well to gain third place. With regard to the Novice events, owing to lack of entries we had to cancel the 100 yards, and only three runners turned out for the 1 Mile. The winner was N. Welsford in moderate time, and it really seems a pity we cannot get a better turn-out in these races. I am sure if only the club members would co-operate we should meet with more success. I trust that if we decide to hold these events in the future that all members will do their best to interest any of their friends who are, as yet, not attached to any recognised athletic club. items.s: THE ANNUAL TRACK WALKS. Report and results of Belgrave's annual promotion of four scratch team walks (5, 3, 2 and 1 miles) at Battersea Park on June 14th, won by Woodford Green A.C. by one point from Belgrave; the 1 mile results print the fourth man's time as 7 min. 4 sec., faster than the winner's 7 min. 16 sec. Our annual promotion of four scratch walks at 5, 3, 2 and 1 miles was held at Battersea Park on June 14th, and nine clubs entered teams. The usual conditions were in force and two men were allowed in each event from each club, no man being allowed to turn out twice in the evening. 18 points were allocated to the winner's club, 17 points to second, and so on, downwards, in each event. The first race was at five miles and Redman (Metropolitan W.C.) and A. H. G. Pope (Woodford Green A.C.) had a spirited duel over the best part of the journey, which carried them well away from the other competitors. Both men are record-holders and their struggle was worthy of the high reputations both men bear in walking circles. Towards the end of the race, Redman drew on his reserves of strength and won by a distance. Our representatives were C. E. Churcher, who finished eighth, and A. Readman, who suffered disqualification. 1, F. Redman (M.W.C.), 37 min. 28 sec.; 2, A. H. Pope (W.G.A.C.) 38 min. 15 sec.; 3, L. P. Hancock (S.W.C.), 39 min. 4 sec.; 4, A. The three miles event followed and in this Whitlock, Olympic Champion, and Cooper, A.A.A. champion, caused some excitement with the mixture of fast and slow walking they provided. Frequent bursts of speed were a feature of the first lap or so, but then Cooper went away to his usual easy win. Our representatives were Charlie Redgrave and Reg. The final event of the evening, a 1 Mile race, was a tussle between Percy Wright and A. H. Rayner (S.A.C.), the last-named prevailing down the straight. Our other man, G. H. We were very glad to welcome eight visiting clubs for our "no entry fee—no award" competition and hope to see them all again next year. items.sum: Report of the annual "Doris" Shield match at Richmond on June 17th, won by Thames Valley H. from Belgrave and Ashcombe-St. George's A.C., with the handicap events for members of the three clubs.
items.s: THE "DORIS" SHIELD CONTEST. Report of the annual "Doris" Shield match at Richmond on June 17th, won by Thames Valley H. from Belgrave and Ashcombe-St. George's A.C., with the handicap events for members of the three clubs. On June 17th we journeyed to Richmond for the annual "Doris" Shield match with Thames Valley H., and Ashcombe-St. George's A.C. We were joint holders of the shield with T.V.H., but any hopes we might have had were rudely dispelled with the result of the 100 yards. Lester and Warner, both of T.V.H., were first and second, with Liffen, of Ashcombe-St. George's, third, and Tom Wiley fourth. In the 440 yards match we had Eddie Pack and he duly won from A. D. G. White, of T.V.H. They also had the third man in R. J. Green, and we were sadly lacking a second string in this race. Tom Wiley, who ran for us, did his best, but was clearly running beyond his distance. We fielded a useful team in the 2 Miles team race and Arthur Penny ran away from his opponents to win in 9 mins. 38 secs. J. C. Smart ran well to finish in second place, while our team was completed by H. G. Verney, the ex-Birchfield runner. The team race result was: Belgrave H., 1; Thames Valley H., 2; Ashcombe-St. George's, 3. With the last event to be decided our chances of even sharing the shield were gone, and Thames Valley consolidated their lead by winning the 1 Mile medley relay. Alec White beat Alby Bird over the half-mile stage, and although Dick Michael ran well in the 440 yards leg, Les. Bennett and S. C. Botwright could not hold the T.V.H. sprinters. Thus the final points scored were: Thames Valley H., 30; Belgrave H., 22; Ashcombe-St. George's A.C., 14. In the usual handicaps open to members of the three competing clubs, we saw J. Warner (who was second in the scratch race) receiving 7½ yards start and he won in 9 4-5 secs. A Belgrave junior in W. H. Bowers was second, off 10 yards, with a T.V.H. youngster, also off 10 yards, third. It was in every respect a long marker's race and the back men, to put it frankly, did not stand an "earthly." A small field was seen in the 2 Miles Walk, there being six Belgrave competitors and one Thames Valley man. Our Walking Hon. Sec., Alf Harley, walked well, however, to win, with Don Brown second, and Harry Churcher, off the scratch mark, third. A better race was seen in the 1 Mile handicap, and on the final lap it looked as if W. R. King, of T.V.H., off 135 yards, would be the winner. E. J. Selby, of the "Bels," off 115 yards, thought otherwise, however. Tommy Morrell, off 90 yards, also put in a spectacular finish and eventually King was placed third. Frank Webb, off 35 yards, ran well to finish a close fourth in what was quite a fast-run race. items.label: August 1937
items.sum: Report and full results of the Belgrave club championship day on July 3rd, 1937, covering track, walk, field and junior events and a schools' medley relay won by Latymer Upper School.
items.s: CLUB CHAMPIONSHIP DAY, July 3rd, 1937. Report and full results of the Belgrave club championship day on July 3rd, 1937, covering track, walk, field and junior events and a schools' medley relay won by Latymer Upper School. We were certainly blesssed with fine weather on our Championship Day, and the performances, if not brilliant, were sound; and the finishes very close and keenly fought out. A new holder had to be found for the Boys, under 15, race, owing to the age limit, and A. V. Heitman, the winner, is full of promise. The newly-instituted 100 yards Junior race gave F. J. Skelley a chance to show his sprinting powers. In view of his successes at the Long Jump, we can certainly expect even better jumping, consequent upon his improved speed. In the 100 yards championship, E. Gray once again proved the best of our short distance men, and retained his hold on the "Grosvenor Cup." Tom Wiley gained one of his many place medals. He picked up four in all—quite a field day! We had been promised a good race in the 880 yards, and so it proved. Alby Bird ran finely to win in time which equalled Tommy Scrimshaw's record of 1 min. 59 1-5 sec. L. W. Herbert was a good second; and Dick Michael, the holder, had to be content with third place. For the first time we held a Junior 880 yards race, and although there was only a small field, it was a most interesting contest. H. G. Neve proved the winner. L. Marchant, who was second, is only 16 years of age, but with careful training should make them all go in a few years' time. As usual, the Mile provided the spectators with an exciting race, and a field of 18 faced the starter. Les Cohen soon showed that he was determined to keep in front; but W. E. Lucas hung on grimly, while our old war-horse, Arthur Penny, was not far behind. Round the last lap they went, but try as he would, Lucas could not get by, and down the straight Cohen strode away to win in 4 min. 33 secs. The 220 yards Junior saw the holder, B. Saunders, show a clean pair of heels to his rivals, although G. K. Talbot ran well to finish second, while R. S. Turner followed up his third in the 100, by filling the same position here. We had a surprise result in the 220 yards championship, for the holder, E. Gray, was beaten a foot by S. C. Botwright, who followed up his recent "Open" successes by annexing the "Elsie Cup." Botwright is a former club junior champion and gives promise of even better performances in the future. Owing to our date clashing with the Police championships, we were denied the sight of Eddie Pack beating the club record of 51 secs. in the 440 yards championship. The race, however, provided us with the closest finish of the day. Alby Bird and L. W. Herbert came down the straight locked together; and Alby gained the verdict by inches. Dick Michael lost another of his titles here, but ran well to finish a close third. Tommy Scrimshaw made a come-back in this race and gave us all a thrill by leading up to the home straight. We all hope to see Tommy once again racing fit, and he certainly has plenty of racing years left in him yet. The 2 Miles Walk saw the holder, W. A. Treacher, and Harry Churcher both non-starters. Don Brown, however, showed he is coming back to his best form by beating Percy Wright, with Joe Coleman pipping his young brother for third place. A feature of this race was the number of ex-runners competing (no offence meant!) and even our Percy has been seen tearing up the sprinters! Our five field event championships saw some good performances, and here again soundness of effort predominated. F. Grassau was an absentee from the Shot Putt and Bill Sutton gained first place with 35ft. 3in. Ben May gained his first place medal here and should gain encouragement from this. In the Javelin, C. A. Melchior became first holder of the "Dailey Cup" with a throw of 155ft. 8in.; and concentration on this particular event would see further improvement. The High Jump saw the holder, H. M. Quackenbos, who is our Junior Captain, retain his title with a leap of 5ft. 2in.; and here again increased height can be expected. "Bud" Hutchinson was second, and with more serious training might show us some of his Canadian form. S. Jones won the Discus Throw with Bill Sutton as runner-up. In fact one might say "the old firm" did their stuff! Another "Dailey Cup" was awarded to the winner of the Long Jump, and we are very grateful to the donor for these welcome additions to our club trophy list. F. J. Skelley, with a fine leap of 21ft. 6in., became the first holder of the cup, and E. Gray also jumped well with an effort of 20ft. 5in. The fact of Gray and Wiley being placed proves once again that speed is essential in this branch of sport. Jesse Owens is, of course, of course the most classic example, and I hope our junior long-jumpers will remember this most important factor. We had another event on our programme which proved quite a success, namely, a 1 Mile medley relay open to Schools. Six teams competed, and the Latymer Upper School ran home winners, due, in the main to a very fine run by their half-miler. This race was in the nature of an experiment and the result was gratifying to those who had urged its inclusion. We hope that next year we shall have an even bigger entry and so help develop the latent talent that these schools must possess. We trust our worthy Hon. Editor was wearing his "old school tie," and are sure he must have been pleased with his old school's victory. The number of standard medals gained in the various club championhips showed the interest that is taken in these awards, but we should like to see even greater interest, and trust that next year will see more club members entering these events. items.label: August 1937
items.sum: Account of the club outing to Littlehampton on Sunday, July 4th, attended by about forty members and friends, praising Mick Walker's handling of an emergency on the journey.
items.s: THE CLUB OUTING. Account of the club outing to Littlehampton on Sunday, July 4th, attended by about forty members and friends, praising Mick Walker's handling of an emergency on the journey. A trip to Littlehampton was planned on Sunday, July 4th, and received a fair measure of support, about forty members and friends contributing to the gaiety of the occasion. Clouds threatened and a strong wind did its best to upset the party, but fortunately there was no rain. Football, cricket, rounders, swimming, rock-climbing (ask Footer!) passed the time, and contributed those aches and pains which were a feature of the next day. However, the trip was generally voted to be an excellent day out; and we record our grateful thanks to our Social Hon. Secretary for his work in connection with the outing. Deserving of special mention is the promptitude and celerity with which Mick Walker met a sudden emergency on the journey outwards. His quickness of thought and physical advantages combined to make him the man of the moment, and to transcend the now almost legendary Colley Hill incident with which the name of Shields is for ever linked. Mick Walker Mick Walker Shields Shields linked with the "Colley Hill incident" Littlehampton Colley Hill

items.label: August 1937
items.sum: Report of the club meeting on July 14th: a junior match with Thames Valley Harriers, won by Belgrave 3 events to 1, and club handicaps on track, walk and javelin.
items.s: THE CLUB MEETING ON JULY 14th. Report of the club meeting on July 14th: a junior match with Thames Valley Harriers, won by Belgrave 3 events to 1, and club handicaps on track, walk and javelin. On this evening we had a Junior match with our old friends, the Thames Valley Harriers, and also several club handicaps. The match events were to be on relay lines, but in the 100 yards event T.V.H. were only able to field two boys, and so we made it a scratch race only. F. J. Skelley won readily enough from W. L. Kuy, of T.V.H., with Belgrave filling the third and fourth positions. In the 880 yards Team race J. Bavage, of T.V.H., a very useful runner, won in 2 mins. 7 secs. They also had the second lad, with H. G. Neve, N. C. Shrubb, L. Marchant, all of Belgrave, in the 3rd, 4th and 5th positions. Thames Valley thus won the team race, and the score was "one all." Skelley did not jump for us in the Junior Long Jump, but the winner was a Belgrave lad, A. S. Peverell, who jumps with a good style and should certainly improve with steady training. The Thames Valley boy was second, with R. Dunford third. The final event was the 3 x 200 yards relay, and over the first leg G. K. Talbot gave us a useful lead. V. D. Wynyard went next, but Bavage, for T.V.H., slowly cut down his advantage. Wynyard held on, to send Skelley away in front of his rival. The latter ran well and did not give his opponent a chance to be on terms. We thus won the match by 3 events to 1, and are looking forward to the return match later in the season. In the 100 yards (under 16) handicap, a close final was seen, the scratch man, L. F. Barber, being beaten by inches by P. McMahon, off 8 yards; S. A. Bailey, off 1 yard, was third; with P. Kearney, Jnr., off 7, fourth. The 100 yards Veterans resulted in a win for A. V. Chetland; with H. H. Baumann, off scratch, second; and Dicky Best, third. Charlie Cook was also in the final, but did not display his customary "dash." For excitement the 880 yards handicap wanted some beating. First, Harry Shields, off 35 yards, looked like winning, but appeared to have made his effort too soon. Then A. H. Beaumont, off 65, went in front, only to be passed in the last few yards by S. Garland, off 42. The final placings were: Garland, Beaumont, Shields, with W. J. Ashford fourth. The 220 yards final was also a close affair, a few yards covering the five finalists. E. A. Keyworth, off 17 yards, proved the winner, with Alby Bird, off 12, second; and R. Shepherd, a junior, off 18, third. Dick Michael was a close fourth and Frank Webb was the other finalist. For three recognised half-milers to figure in a sprint final does not say much for the quality of our sprinters; but perhaps the handicapper was kind to them! Anyway, we will leave it at that! A good race was also seen in the club 2 Miles Walk handicap, J. A. Belchamber, a son of our past President, making good use of his 525 yards start, to lead until half-way round the last lap, where E. C. A. Heather, off 350 yards—a liberal mark—caught him although he only won by a few yards. Joe Coleman walked excellently off 175 yards to gain third place; with his brother "L.J." once again close behind him. There was a good field for the 2 Miles running handicap and another long-marker in W. F. Merryman, off 420, led throughout, to win in fast time. R. W. Tobin, off 300 yards, secured his first club prize in finishing second; and Pat Parker ran a really magnificent race to gain third place. He did 9 mins. 31 secs. all the way; form which augured well for his chance in the A.A.A. 3 Miles race the following Saturday. H. G. Verney also ran well to finish in fifth place, while Les Cohen was seventh off the scratch mark. He had to give Pat 5 yards start; but perhaps the boot will be on the other foot in the next handicap we have. Members of the running section gained first two awards in the Javelin throw handicap. S. Garland, with 65 feet allowance, was first; and Mick Walker, with 60 feet start, gained second place. Both Finneron and Melchior, also George Powell, were non-starters, otherwise the result might have been different. We are pleased, however, to see members outside the field events men themselves, taking part in these contests; and if they pay their share of the entry fees it is only right they should take their share of the prizes, too. Also on the programme was a 1 Mile Walk for Unattached Novices, but there were only two starters, the winner being W. F. Brunning, who we hope will not be discouraged by his lack of opposition. Why these novice events should fail to attract entries is really mystifying, unless, of course, there are no unattached men, all being members of the Belgrave, which is as it should be! F. J.
