items.label: February 1938
items.h: The South of the Thames "Junior Race."
items.sum: F. R. Webb's report of the South of the Thames Junior cross-country race on 13th November, won by Eastleigh Town S.C., with Belgrave's "A" team fifth.
e: South of the Thames Junior Cross Country Championship
items.s: The South of the Thames "Junior Race." F. R. Webb's report of the South of the Thames Junior cross-country race on 13th November, won by Eastleigh Town S.C., with Belgrave's "A" team fifth. BY F. R. WEBB. Saturday, 13th November. Whether it was the date, or lack of voices with that familiar cry of "Up the Bels" was responsible for our team's failure to get placed in the above race I cannot say; but the support they did have must have been the poorest ever. However, the few that did go witnessed a most exciting race. The course, which was one of three laps consisting mainly of grassland. Harry Parker, one of the Club's officials, being President of the South of the Thames Association, had the honour of starting the race. It was also hoped that he would present the Shield to our Club as the winning team, but it did not materialise. Our boys got away fairly well and the field, having covered about half a mile of level going, came to a stretch of plough. After getting over this, they then continued out into the country, and thence back to the starting field, which was preceded by a slight rise, which upset those who had made too fast a start. The first to appear was a bunch of about six runners. A little further back came Tobin in 12th position, followed by Lucas 19th, Morrell 22nd, and Murdoch 36th. Our next man was round about the 50 mark. On their next appearance they had covered about 3 miles, and Roberts, of Mitcham, was leading by a few yards from Isted, of Westerham ,and Shirley, of Ashcombe. Our boys had failed to improve their positions. In fact, they had lost some! Tobin was still our first man, and had lost a few places, as had Lucas and Morrell. Murdoch had gained, so had Clements and Stride. These two were running very strongly and we still hoped there might be a chance of a place. Herbert and Selby were definitely below their usual form, running in 102nd and 113th positions. Johnson, who was in the "B" team, was going very strongly in the 80th position. Again the runners entered the starting field and commenced the last lap; but no claret and gold vests could be seen in the first twenty places. So came the end, with Clements running strongly over the last lap to finsh 18th. Tobin (24th), Murdock (25th) and Lucas (26th) completed our team, which was placed 5th. Eastleigh Town S.C., who owe much to our old friend Tommy Green, were the winners. As previously mentioned, our "A" team finished fifth with 93 points. Our "B" team scored 410 points, and "C" team 663. There were 270 starters, 254 of whom finished the course. F. R. Webb F. R. Webb Harry Parker Harry Parker President of the South of the Thames Association; started the race Tobin Tobin 24th Lucas Lucas 26th Morrell Morrell Murdoch Murdoch 36th early in the race Murdock Murdock 25th Roberts Roberts leading at about 3 miles Isted Isted Shirley Shirley Clements Clements 18th, first Belgrave finisher Stride Stride Herbert Herbert 102nd at about 3 miles Selby Selby 113th at about 3 miles Johnson Johnson "B" team; 80th at about 3 miles Tommy Green Tommy Green "our old friend"; Eastleigh Town S.C. owe much to him South of the Thames Junior Cross Country Championship Mitcham Westerham Ashcombe Eastleigh Town S.C.

items.label: February 1938
items.sum: Report of the inter-club race with Mitcham A.C. from Belgrave Hall, won by Belgrave 364 pts. to 456 with Arthur Penny first home.
items.s: Inter-Club Race with Mitcham A.C. Report of the inter-club race with Mitcham A.C. from Belgrave Hall, won by Belgrave 364 pts. to 456 with Arthur Penny first home. This fixture took the place of the usual four-cornered social run with Croydon H., Epsom H. and Mitcham A.C. It has been decided to hold one fixture each season, this to take place in turn from each club's quarters. Owing to Mitcham's quarters being on the small side, we held this year's race from "Belgrave Hall"; and a good crowd was seen out, although Epsom and Croydon were unable to field sufficiently large numbers to count in the team race. So we had a race with the Mitcham boys and, scoring 20 aside, came out on top by 364 pts. to 456 pts. First man home was Arthur Penny; followed by S. O. A. Palmer and R. Thorogood, both of Mitcham. Then came Tom Carter, Les Cohen and Harry Verney, of the "Bels"; followed by L. Scott, of Mitcham, with that old war-horse Bert Footer next. After that, positions were more or less equally divided between the two clubs, although our boys seemed to pack in small groups and this undoubtedly helped when the final scores were worked out. Whether we can take this as a good omen as regards the later "big" races remains to be seen, as in fairness to Mitcham we must say that they did not have their full complement of Welshmen running for them in this race, and there is no doubt that the influx of their "Hospital" boys makes them a much more formidable proposition. items.s: Race v. Highgate H. and R.A.F., Uxbridge. Report of the November 27th match at De Bohun's Farm, Southgate, won by Cpl. Hier of the R.A.F., in which Belgrave dead-heated with Highgate Harriers in the team race. On November 27th we visited De Bohun's Farm, Southgate, for a match with Highgate Harriers; and fellow visitors were the R.A.F., Uxbridge, and the Metropolitan Police A.C. In a race over six miles, Cpl. Hier, of the R.A.F., came home an easy winner, and will prove an asset to Surrey A.C. when the open races come along. Tom Carter finished second with E. W. Bourne, of Highgate, third; and in the team race we dead-heated with the home club, each side scoring 112 pts. The R.A.F. scored 212, and the Police 354. Dick Tobin ran well to be our second man home, followed by G. Murdock and Tom Morrell. Nine aside scored in the team race, and we were very pleased to renew old associations by this pleasant fixture. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: Report and results of the Club 7 Miles cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield on December 11th, run over 6 miles against visitors L'Union Sportive Metropolitaine of Paris, won by A. W. Penny with R. E. Stride, Jnr. winning the sealed handicap.
items.s: The Club 7 Miles C.C. Championship. Report and results of the Club 7 Miles cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield on December 11th, run over 6 miles against visitors L'Union Sportive Metropolitaine of Paris, won by A. W. Penny with R. E. Stride, Jnr. winning the sealed handicap. On December 11th we held the Club 7 Miles Championship for the "Blackstaffe" Shield, with the usual sealed handicap in conjunction. This year, however, marked a very special occasion, none other than the first visit of a foreign club to compete against our boys on their own soil. At the visitors' request the course was one of 6 miles, but the Committee decided that it should still rule as the Club Championship, and so this year's winner of the "Blackstaffe" Shield had less distance to run than usual. Our visitors were the runners of the L'Union Sportive Metropolitaine, Paris. They sent 7 men and so it was decided to score 6 men aside in the team race. The course was the usual one of 2 laps, but, as explained, it was shortened slightly by cutting off a piece out in the country, so that from a spectator's point of view the runners were seen at the usual points of vantage. On the first lap the Frenchmen broke away in a body to go in front, but Pat Parker soon strode ahead only to give way to Arthur Penny and when they came round the first time, Arthur was well in front and running strongly. Dan Patience had come up to Pat Parker, and then came Les Cohen and Bert Footer followed by Tom Carter and then the Frenchmen, running more or less in a solid bunch. When they came in sight again at the Windmill, Arthur Penny was still leading, with Dan Patience a comfortable second, and Pat Parker third. Les Cohen and Bert Footer were still close together, but four of the "Metro" boys had come up to Carter's shoulder, and the leader of them appeared quite fresh. In the run home the positions remained unchanged but Tom Carter fought well, and although having to give way to two of his rivals he managed to fight off the others and finished just in front of three more "Metro" lads. Thus although the Frenchmen packed very well it was too far back to give any chance of success in the team race. With the first five men home our position was unassailable, and our captain, Tom Carter, completed our scoring team of six men which we had in the first eight positions. We are sure, however, that our very good friends from Paris learnt a wrinkle or two which should stand them in good stead in future races. The winner of the sealed handicap was a very promising young runner, R. E. Stride, Jnr., and on his running in the scratch race, he well deserved his victory. J. C. Smart, who is a first-claim member of the Orion Harriers, finished second on handicap; while third place was gained by Dick Michael, who is better known as a track runner. With a Tea and Social Evening after the run we thus ended what was quite an event in the history of our Club, and hope that in future years we may hold events of a similar nature, which do much to cement the good feeling and fellowship between athletes of different countries. items.s: The Surrey County C.C. Championship. Report and result of the Surrey County cross-country championship, won by Mitcham A.C. with Belgrave second, followed by a note on Belgrave runners in the Inter-counties Championship at Gatton Park. The most important feature of this year's Championship was that, after many years in our possession, the title passed into another club's keeping—and Mitcham A.C. are the present holders. This was Mitcham's first win and the manner of their winning calls for the heartiest congratulations. They supplied the individual champion, the third man home, and completed their team in 19 scoring positions—excellent running. We were sixteen points behind, and then came a huge gap and Thames Hare and Hounds in third position with over double our number of points. Our team was not disgraced, and our performance of placing twelve men in the first 53 scoring positions was very satisfying. RESULT. * * * * * A fortnight later A. W. Penny and H. E. Footer figured in the winning Surrey team in the Inter-counties Championship held at Gatton Park, and D. Patience scored in the Middlesex team, placed third. C. T. Carter also represented Surrey, and R. W. Tobin figured in the Middlesex nine. Harry Verney, who was expected to run in the Middlesex team, was forced to stand down owing to a knee injury received in France the previous week. m. s. 1 R. Thorogood M.A.C. 45 18 2 S. C. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: T. J. Flower's report and result of the Middlesex cross-country championship at Folly Farm, New Barnet, where Cadogan A.C. (Belgrave) regained the Daily Telegraph Cup with 84 points and F. L. Mason of T.V.H. won; the report's placings (17th, 22nd) differ from the printed result (18th, 23rd).
items.s: Middlesex Cross Country Championship. T. J. Flower's report and result of the Middlesex cross-country championship at Folly Farm, New Barnet, where Cadogan A.C. (Belgrave) regained the Daily Telegraph Cup with 84 points and F. L. Mason of T.V.H. won; the report's placings (17th, 22nd) differ from the printed result (18th, 23rd). It was a long trek to "Folly Farm," New Barnet, but well worth the trip, as our "boys" regained the "Daily Telegraph" Cup, after a very keen and exciting race . We were all feeling fairly confident before the race, and although Alf Taylor had to drop out early in the race through leg trouble, it seemed to add zest to the others. The spectators saw quite a lot of the race, and with very little effort on our part we were able to see the run at five different stages. The race started in a mad dash and after first 700 yards had been covered, Cpl. Hier and J. Bain led the field. They went out of sight into the woods at this point and we waited patiently for their return. Cpl. Hier still led with Bain, and Mason about 15 yards behind. 50 yards further away came D. Patience (4th) and he appeared to be running very strongly. Then they came thick and fast, but to my surprise Tobin was our second man in the 7th position. Verney was 11th, R. Patience 12th, Smart 23rd, J. Flower 28th, Shields 33rd—very satisfactory for the half-way stage. 85 points for 6—with another close up—was very cheering indeed, and they kept these position round the field and so out again into the woods. On entering, the field for the last 700 yards of the race, F. L. Mason, of T.V.H, held a lead of about 12 yards and running in beautiful style and very fast, gradually drew away from J. Bain, last year's champion, who ran a very gallant race, game to the very end. Unfortunately for him he met a man at the top of his form, who finished not only very strongly but comparatively fresh—a worthy "Champion of Middlesex." After this excitement, I concentrated on the Team Race. D. Patience, after a ding-dong battle over the last 700 yards, forced his way to a 10 yards lead over C. W. Griffiths (an ex-champion of Middlesex) and so finished in the 4th position. Very gratifying to myself, waiting to collect the discs! Then came a T.V.H. man (7th), closely followed by Verney (8th) and Tobin (9th). Then two more "Valley" men, 12th and 16th, D. Patience for the "Cads" very close up, 17th, then J. E. Flower 22nd, followed by yet another "Valley" man, 23rd; and what a relief, Shields and Smart, 25th and 26th respectively. A rapid addition of points gave us 84. The T.V.H. scorer, standing beside me, said, "Our boys scored 96, how did you do, Cadogan?" Feeling as proud as if I had actually scored in the team, I replied, "84 and I think we've won it!" "Well done! and congratulations to your lads," was his reply—very typical of the sporting crowd they are! There was sympathy for Smart, who after running a very plucky race, just missed the winning team by one second. To him I say, "Better luck next time! it's your turn next!" A. Patience surprised the natives by his storming finish. He was told (wrongly) that he was 6th man and he put in a tremendous effort, gaining 15 or more places over the last 700 yards. A. Smith put up his best performance in this race. And so for home, feeling quite content in spite of the rain and a 20 minutes' walk to the station. RESULT. A. E. Taylor did not finish. m. s. 1 F. L. items.label: February 1938
items.h: The International Cross-Country Race at la Croix de Berny, Paris, on 16th January, 1938.
items.sum: Account of Belgrave's trip to Paris for the international cross-country race at la Croix de Berny on 16th January 1938, where the team, the only British entry, finished third behind U.S. Belfortaine and C.O. Billancourt.
e: International Cross-Country Race, la Croix de Berny
items.s: The International Cross-Country Race at la Croix de Berny, Paris, on 16th January, 1938. Account of Belgrave's trip to Paris for the international cross-country race at la Croix de Berny on 16th January 1938, where the team, the only British entry, finished third behind U.S. Belfortaine and C.O. Billancourt. A further invitation having been given by the Union Sportive Metropolitaine for us to compete in the above event was accepted and the following team was chosen to represent the Club: Carter, Cohen, Footer, Patience D., Parker, Penny, Tobin and Verney, accompanied by W. G. Webb and H. Parker as Club Officials. Unfortunately, a very rough crossing awaited the party that left London on Friday, 15th January, and on their arrival in Paris on the Saturday morning all were glad to take a few hours' rest. After an early lunch the party made a rather extensive tour of Paris in a coach kindly provided by the French Club; and later adjourned to their Hotel for tea, and to discuss Bert Footer's programme for their evening's entertainment. It was quite evident that Mr. Footer knew his Paris well and did not require the services of an interpreter who had been placed at the party's disposal. The President and Mrs. Bayliss, accompanied by Mr. Togna, joined the company early in the evening and soon we were to hear the voices of our President, Tom Carter, Bert Footer and Arthur Penny coming over the air from the Radio City Broadcasting Station in Paris, telling the French folk why the Belgrave Harriers were in their gay city. Soon after breakfast on Sunday we were speeding on our way to the Headquarters of the Union Sportive Metropolitaine at le Croix de Berny. This famous organisatiaon caters for sport of all kinds and its hundreds of acres of land all set our for sport are indeed wonderful. I doubt if there is anything like it to be seen in this country. The Club House is a huge building and soon we were taking lunch with hundreds of other competitors. 38 teams were to compete in the Internationl Cross Country Race which included the Belgian Champions (Union St-Gilloise) and Belgrave Harriers as the only British entry. After the parade of the runners the "Off" was given and soon we had the pleasure of seeing Parker leading the field, with the rest of the team, excepting Verney, lying quite handy. Verney, it must be explained, had developed a temperature, and though he persisted in turning out, it was very evident that he was unwell. At 3 miles Parker was still leading, with Penny and Footer coming through to the front. At this stage it seemed, however, that our boys were further back than they should be and one began to wonder if that awful sea-crossing was affecting their running. At 5 miles Parker had dropped to 5th place, and though Penny and Footer were running strongly, and Carter and Cohen striving hard, it could easily be seen that we could not win. The team of Algerians (U.S. Belfortaine) was running wonderfully well, and had 3 men in the first four. Our boys ran very pluckily, however, and were beaten by the narrow margin of 5 points for second place. In the last lap of the race, Penny came up to pass Parker and finished first man for us in the 7th position. Parker finished 9th, Footer 11th, Carter 23rd, Cohen 27th, Tobin 32nd, Patience 34th, and Verney continued gamely to finish 117th. The first team placings were as follows:— I understand that during the race our President was introduced to members of the German, Austrian and Italian Governments. Are the Belgrave Harriers to visit one of these countries for International Honours? I wonder! 1. U.S. Belfortaine 68 points. 2. C.O. Billancourt 104 points. 3. Belgrave Harriers 109 points. 4. Union St. Gilloise 186 points. Carter Carter 23rd Cohen Cohen 27th Footer Footer 11th Patience D. Patience D. Parker Parker led early; finished 9th Penny Penny first Belgrave man home, 7th Tobin Tobin 32nd Verney Verney ran with a temperature; finished 117th W. G. Webb W. G. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: Report of the club's Boxing Day track meeting at Battersea Park, with a 120 yds. sprint handicap, a 3 miles walking handicap, a 2 miles run and a field event match with the Metropolitan Police A.C.
items.s: The Club Boxing Day Meeting. Report of the club's Boxing Day track meeting at Battersea Park, with a 120 yds. sprint handicap, a 3 miles walking handicap, a 2 miles run and a field event match with the Metropolitan Police A.C. At Battersea Park on Boxing Day morning we held our annual track meeting and, being blessed with fine weather, we had a good crowd and, what is more important, good entries. First came the heats in the 120 yds. sprint handicap and the winners were: Heat 1, A. S. Blunden (5 yds.); Heat 2, S. Lyons (7); Heat 3, A. Mewes (6); Heat 4, F. J. Skelley (5). This pointed to a good final, the odds being slightly in favour of Lyons, a new member, and so it turned out. Skelley ran finely but could not make up his two yards deficit and Stan Blunden was close on his shoulder. The winner looks a very promising sprinter and, provided he does not overdo matters too early in the season, he should prove a very useful addition to our sprint team. The 3 Miles walking handicap provided a rather poor field (that is, numerically) and "Ginger" Coleman had no difficulty in winning from Reg. Elson, with a promising young walker in A. E. Elliott, third. Joe Coleman came under the ban of the judges when well placed, while Percy Wright found his Christmas festivities too much for him and retired. We are indebted to Mr. Askew for so kindly presenting a consolation prize in the fourth walker, the only pity being that there were not more members of the walking section there to battle for it. It must, of course, be borne in mind that several walkers were at Croydon, contesting the annual 18¾ miles Boxing Day Walk. As usual, at this meeting, the most eagerly awaited event was the 2 miles run and a large field turned out for this. George Still was on the limit mark, while Arthur Penny was virtual scratch with 10 yards. George kept in front for several laps but the field gradually overhauled him and with a lap to go things looked very interesting. Arthur Penny had come through in great style but still had a good leeway to make up on the leaders. Dick Tobin was in front with A. Harper hanging on his shoulder and A. H. Orton coming up very fast in third place . Down the straight Tobin increased his lead and Orton could not quite catch Harper, while "Champ" Smith had run well to get fourth position. Arthur Penny finished very strongly and Bert Shaw just pipped him for fifth place, which, considering how close he was to the winner, made Arthur doing a very good performance. In conjunction with the racing events we had a Field Event match with the Metropolitan Police A.C., there being three events and scoring for the first six places in each. We triumphed in the Shot Putt by 11 pts. to 10, S. Jones, of the "Bels," having the best putt of 37ft. 5ins. In the Javelin we again came out on top, this time by 12pts. to 9, and C. A. Melchior had the best throw of 143ft. 2ins., with George Powell third. The final event was the Discus and in this the Police had the first three men and so scored 15 pts. to our 6, their best man being W. Grigg, with 123ft. 6ins. Thus in the final points we lost to the Police by 5 points, they scoring 34 to our 29, but I am sure all those who took part were well satisfied with what was the first fixture to take place at this time of the year, and we look forward to holding a similar contest next year. items.s: Winding Up The Country Season. Comment by the running secretary on the cross-country season so far, the coming South of Thames, Southern Counties and National championships, road fixtures, and the clash of the News of the World London–Brighton relay's new date with the Club Dinner. So far this season, results have not been as we hoped they would, but with the real Championship tests now coming along, we hope that our lads will prove their supremacy over the country. Actually our runners, both Juniors and Seniors, have performed very well; and in the three Surrey County races we have recorded a treble of second places which to some clubs would be very pleasing. Also our members with Middlesex qualifications scored a win in their County race, while running for their second-claim club. The next championship in which we compete will be the South of Thames "Senior" race to be held at Cobham. The course there is rather a heavy one, and not likely to suit our boys, while owing to the numerous and, might I say, tedious barring clauses, we are debarred from fielding what can be termed a representative team. We come then to the Southern Counties Championships (both Senior and Junior) which will be held at Ascot. Shades of "Brown Jack"! What is the world coming to? Alas! the modern trend is to make cross-country running easier in every way. They even have artificial obstacles, and quite possibly they will one year stage a race indoors at Wembley! Seriously, though, there is quite a lot to be said for such a venue as Ascot. The dressing accommodation, with the consequent after-the-race facilities, should be A.1, and I am all in favour of anything which is to the benefit of the competing athlete. The spectators should also have a good view of the proceedings, and the "gate" will also benefit the Association, which possibly is the reason for this hankering after race-courses as venues. In the Junior race I am afraid our team will be rather weak, as R. E. Stride and Bill Lucas, who were our first two home in our club Junior championship, are now both over age. It should, however, provide useful experience to the rest of our Juniors, and we wish them the best of luck. As to the Senior race, we must expect hot opposition from Mitcham A.C. and Surrey A.C. At first glance, Mitcham would appear favourites, but Surrey should not be disregarded, and they usually put up a good performance in this race. With our best team in the field we should, however, give them all a rare old battle and we will leave it by saying "may the best team win." On March 12th the E.C.C.U. hold the "National" championship and this year the race will be staged at Coley Park, Reading. We can be assured that the local committee will make arrangements for everybody, and I hope our Club supporters will travel to Reading on the 12th to see what is, without doubt, the finest cross-country race of the Season. Special buses will run from the station to Coley Park, and the course is one which gives the spectators a constant view of the runners. Last year we lost the title by 4 points, the holders, Birchfield Harriers, having a rare fright before they found victory was theirs once again. This year, we hope the tide will turn, and that we shall regain the trophy which we held in 1935. Our teams have, in recent years, always seemed to give of their best in this race; and we hope that Tom Carter, in his first season as Captain, will have the honour of leading them to victory. I am sure all our lads will give him their loyal support. With such names as Penny, Footer, Ginty, Parker, D. Patience, Carter and Cohen to think of, it will be seen that we have every chance of success to bring the title where it has so seldom been in late years, namely the South. On March 19th will be held the "Round Ilford" Road Relay, and we hope to enter teams, as in past years, and so give all our members a chance of representing the club in "open" team competition. The country season is now at on end and we start road training with a view to the London—Brighton Relay race. On April 9th we had decided to hold our usual 5 miles Road Race with sealed handicap in conjunction, but whether this date will be changed in view of the alteration of "Brighton" date, will have to be advised to members later. In any case I hope all our members will support this fixture at Wimbledon, for as mentioned, there is the handicap to go for, and I shall be glad to receive entries in good time before the date fixed for this race. We now come to what is for us a rather unfortunate happening and that is the fact that the "News of the World," after fixing April 30th for their annual "classic," have at this late date suddenly altered the date to May 7th. It is understood that it is owing to clashing with the annual Stock Exchange walk to Brighton, although why this question was not gone into when the date was first fixed is to be wondered at. As our members are aware, May 7th is the date arranged for our Club Dinner and naturally we cannot expect to have half the club at "Gatti's" and half at Brighton. The matter will be discussed by our Committee and what will happen remains to be seen. It would be a thousand pities if we did not compete in this year's race, after being winners for three consecutive years—a feat not previously accomplished in the history of this event. We lost last year by a bare few yards to Mitcham and had looked forward to reversing this result. Our absence from the race might be misconstrued by some, and it is to be hoped that we shall be able to arrange to compete, although very galling, and absolutely lacking in consideration. items.s: A Message From Paris. Covering letter from Paris enclosing the proof of an article for the "Metro Sportif" magazine, followed by that article on the Union Sportive Metropolitaine team's visit to the Belgrave Harriers at Wimbledon. My Dear Sir, I send you herewith the "proof" of an article that I am having inserted in the next number of our magazine, the "Metro Sportif." It is an article concerning our meeting with the Belgrave Harriers, and I would thank you very much if you would be kind enough to check me up on the details that I have mentioned. I hope you will excuse me for troubling you and meanwhile I beg you to accept my sincere thanks and my most cordial wishes, etc., etc. WITH OUR FRIENDS AT WIMBLEDON. THE BELGRAVE HARRIERS. One will read further on, under the heading of "Cross Country," an article describing the visit of our team to England on the 10, 11, 12 December, where they were the guests of the Belgrave Harriers, who, you will remember, were our guests last season at La Croix de Berny. It is not the time or place to criticise the result of our match, which left no illusions, but rather to analyse and see what useful purpose has been gained by our visit, and a reception that will certainly go down to posterity in the annals of our Cross Country section. To give you some idea of how formidable were our opponents, I am going to give you some details. First of all, let us remember that the Belgrave Harriers specialise in athletics, walking and, above all, cross country running. Founded in 1887, they, along with the Birchfield Harriers, are reckoned among the top flight of clubs in England. They were cross country champions of England in 1935, winners of the London to Brighton relay race for 1934, 35, 36, winners of the Surrey County Championship from 1925 to 1937, and this year further added to their laurels by capturing our cross-country championship at La Croix de Berny in 1937. Their Patron is Sir Samuel Hoare, former Secretary of State at the Foreign Office, and former First Lord of the Admiralty, now Home Secretary, who combines this presidency with that of the Lawn Tennis Association of Great Britain. Their active President and Hon. Secy. is our excellent friend, Mr. W. L. Bayliss, who has never failed to put at our disposal his kindly services. The Belgrave Harriers have more than five hundred active members. Their training ground is situated at Wimbledon, a south-western suburb of London which has a population of 65,000 inhabitants, and which is world-famous on account of its famous tennis stadium. Wimbledon, situated at only 15 kilometres from the heart of London, is served by the Southern Railway and also an underground line. In close proximity there are the "commons" (Putney, Richmond, etc.), fine sandy stretches, sprinkled with woods, and many gradients, which lends itself perfectly to the art and training of cross-country running, and other sports among them being the noble one of "Equitation." Well, here we are with them at Wimbledon. After a wet and unpromising morning a complete change came about mid-day, and the afternoon proved to be fine and cold. Here, on the premises which the Belgrave Harriers have just acquired and which they intend to demolish in order to build a model club house, is a big hall, comfortably heated. On the floor a badminton court is marked out. At the moment this hall also serves as a cloak room and leading off the hall are several baths, simple in style, but comfortable and above all, warm; whilst a little further on one discovers the pantry, where all sorts of good things were prepared for the dinner that we all enjoyed in common with the Belgrave Harriers, and its many friends. items.s: Belgrave H. v. Metropolitan Police. Report and results of the field events match against the Metropolitan Police (shot putt, javelin, discus), lost 29–34 on aggregate; the report says S. Jones beat Grigg in the Weight and Belgrave won it 11–10, while the printed shot putt table places McLennon 1st, Grigg 2nd and Jones 3rd with Police scoring more points. Field Events. Our match with the Police proved a success, each side having full teams for each event. In the Weight, S. Jones beat D. L. Grigg (International) by a small margin, enabling us to win this event by 1 point, the score being Belgrave 11, Police 10. The other placings were closely contested, the distances being comparable with Summer performances. In fact, Jones's winning distance is best to date. The Javelin was won by C. A. Melchior, who beat Grigg by over 6ft., George Powell being a close 3rd. S. Jones scored as our third team man. H. M. Quackenbos, our Junior Captain, had an excellent throw of 12ft. 9in. and was actually placed 7th. L. Jackson had an off day, after throwing over 120 ft. consistently on practice. We scored 12 pts. to Police 9 pts. We were beaten in the Discus, the Police gaining the first 3 positions although without three of their best men. They have to thank Grigg for this, as he has coached them during the Winter months. S. Jones was again our best performer with 98ft., Melchior and W. H. Sutton completing the team. Although we won two of the three events, we lost the match on the aggregate., points being Belgrave 29, Met. Police, 34. Conclusions drawn from this match show that if serious Winter training is maintained, together with similar matches, there should be an appreciable all-round increase of ability to the benefit of the members and the Club. The Police have asked for another match to be held at Imber Court in February. Thanks are due to Mr. F. G. Thomson, who acted as Field Events judge. RESULTS. Name. Club. Distance Pos. Again our walkers gave splendid support to this promotion, and once gain our successes were many. With our scoring four in the first nine positions, the team race was easily won. In fact, with five men in twelve, six in fifteen, and seven in 19, we should have made a good show against all-comers combined! By reason of their forward walking our "A" team also took the second handicap team awards. There was also much good walking forthcoming from our "B" team, but on this occasion they returned without reward. Len Coleman, included in the "A" team, finished 29th, and with a seven minutes' allowance, was placed third in the individual handicap. His rapid improvement has given much satisfaction. items.s: Our "Open" Walk. Report and partial result of Belgrave's eighteenth annual open walk on 27 November, won by H. G. Churcher with Belgrave taking the scratch team race and second handicap team awards. Printed slips kept: W. H. Snell's handicap time 56 54 (sum gives 56 34), F. Jarvis '57221', Metropolitan W.C. '319m. 49s.', and two teams both listed as Belgrave H. (D). The last Saturday in November, the 27th, was once again the occasion of much activity for walkers. Our Eighteenth Annual promotion attracted 182 entries, and 22 teams were nominated. No less than 33 Belgrave walkers entered, and we started four teams. The afternoon was cold, but fortunately the fog that had threatened during the morning had lifted, and conditions were quite good when our President started the race. Our walkers were soon seen to be prominent, with Harry Churcher and Fred Redman, of the Metropolitan W.C., contesting the lead. Round about three miles, Harry broke away up the hill and proceeded to build up a big lead. The gap between second and third men at half-way was considerable. It was obvious at this point that no other club was near us in the scratch team race. Eventually, our lads finished H. G. Churcher (1st), C. E. Churcher (3rd), P. G. Wright (4th) and J. G. Coleman (6th)—a wonderfully fine team effort, and additionally, there was some splendid further support forthcoming. Actually, ridiculous though it seems, in the best-supported Open race of the season, Don Brown finished 8th and yet did not score in the team! Bert Clayton, our new member resident at Eastleigh, gave another good display of walking in finishing eleventh. He will undoubtedly prove a great asset when he qualifies for our teams. Len Coleman again showed his promise, and succeeded in taking an individual handicap prize. In fact, the whole race may be considered a testimony to the Club's strength. The individual handicap was won by E. H. Johnson (8 min. 40 sec.) of Surrey Walking Club and the Stock Exchange—a rapidly improving walker. Second came R. C. Pantling (4 min.) of the London Vidarians' W.C., and this club succeeded in winning the Team Handicap race. Our "A" team took the second handicap awards. The result, which is appended, gives ample evidence of the Club's success in the race. The Churcher family, in particular, did well, taking three prizes each! Before concluding, we should like to pay a tribute and express our grateful thanks to Messrs. W. Allen, Askew, Belchamber, Elson and Gordon, for their generous contributions to the Prize Fund; to the R.W.A. officials and others who helped with the organisation of the race, and without whose help we could not carry on; and to the competitors themselves for their annual support. Report and result of the club junior walk championship for the Horwood Cup over seven miles on 11 December: Harry Churcher first overall, Colin Sutton junior champion, French walker Cambrai sixth, and "Jock" Ogilvie winning the handicap (H. G. Churcher's printed times 55 30 / 9 10 / 56 20 duplicate E. G. Cornish's). On December 11th we had hoped to welcome a team of French walkers to an inter-club event, to be decided with all club members competing and with the Club Junior Championship for the "Horwood" Cup, in conjunction. Unfortunately, as the day approached, our French friends intimated that they would not be able to send a complete team, but that Cambrai, a well-known walker on the other side of the Channel, would represent them. Cambrai quickly went to the front when the Mayor of Wimbledon started the race, in company with our fastest men. He soon found the pace too fast, however, and eventually finished in sixth position. This does not represent his true form, for he has shown some remarkable pace for an hour, and up to 50 kilometres, in Paris. We understood, however, that he had competed in a long-distance race the previous week, and no doubt this occasioned some loss of speed, if a time of 57 min. 25 secs. over our seven miles course deserves this description. The actual winner, Harry Churcher, won reasonably easily from Percy Wright, who made a good show. Then came the "Juniors," battling out the Championship—probably one of the finest fields seen out in this race. After a most strenuous struggle, Colin Sutton gained a narrow win over Joe Coleman. Bert Clayton, our Eastleigh member, took the third medal in his first appearance in the Club Championship. Form throughout was most satisfactory. Len Coleman would probably have given a better performance had he not devoted the previous evening and the Saturday morning to the care of the French visitors, to whom he acted as interpreter. It was pleasing to see a comparative newcomer in "Jock" Ogilvie take the handicap first, with G. S. Doubleday, another newcomer to walking, in third position. Second prize went to Reg Elson, an old-timer showing a welcome return to form. Act. Pos. Junior Champ. Name. H'cap Pos. 1 H. G. Churcher 55 30 9 10 56 20 2 P. G. Wright 56 26 2 25 54 1 3 1 C. F. items.s: The Ashcombe-St. George's A.C. Open Walk. Report and result of the Ashcombe-St. George's A.C. open walk over seven miles from Sheen Schools into Richmond Park on 2 January, where Belgrave took the first five places; several printed handicap times do not agree with actual time minus allowance (H. G. Churcher, R. F. Elson, E. G. Cornish, W. G. True, W. T. Brunning). Held from Sheen Schools over a seven miles course into Richmond Park on January 2nd, our boys showed their liking for familiar roads by recording a truly amazing performance. Recent form has made us expect some good walking from our teams, but to finish the first five men home in a race of this nature is deserving of a welter of superlatives. Harry Churcher scored his usual win in comfortable fashion, and Len and Joe Coleman finished together, equal second. To say that Joe walked wonderfully well is to invite rhapsodic language to describe brother Len's performance and we will content ourselves with reminding our readers that fifteen months previously Len Coleman won a Club novice race! Captain Charlie Churcher finished in fourth position, and Percy Wright was fifth. Actually there is no scratch team race in this particular event (only a set of prizes for fastest team not gaining handicap awards) or Percy would have found himself in the unique position of finishing fifth in an open race, and yet not scoring in his Club team. Reg. Elson confirmed his recent good form by finishing 10th, and here we would like to record our appreciation of the good nature and splendid sportsmanship of one of our second-claim members, W. E. Ives. Elson was awaiting the return of his shoes from the repairer, who had undertaken to have them at the dressing room in time for the race. Unfortunately, he failed in this, and Reg Elson was ready, all but for shoes. Ives, himself stripped ready to race, hearing of the position, insisted upon the faster man using his shoes, with happy results. We are all grateful to Ives for his self-sacrificing action. In the handicap team race our "B" team was second. This team consisted of Doubleday, Ogilvie, Roberts and True, the two first-named taking their first team prizes in Club teams. Our "A" team was placed third; and so we may be considered to have had an excellent Saturday afternoon out. RESULT. 91 finished. items.label: February 1938
items.sum: Walking notes previewing the Junior and Senior championships, reviewing the Boxing Day Godstone walk, with a note from the track captain and the walking fixture list.
items.s: With The Walkers. Walking notes previewing the Junior and Senior championships, reviewing the Boxing Day Godstone walk, with a note from the track captain and the walking fixture list. At this time of the year, all with any interest in walking turn their thoughts towards the "Junior" Championship, to be held this year from Hampstead Garden Suburb, on March 5th. It is not our usual custom to laud our prospects to the skies; but this year we should be false to ourselves if we did not recognise that we have an outstanding team to represent us. The form of past weeks indicates that we have a team which may well set up a new "low-points" record and better the scores of Surrey Walking Club (1929, 22 points), and our score of 1933 (26 points)—the two best yet recorded. Certainly it is true to say that practically every other club expects us to win the Championship once again, and our boys will do their utmost not to disappoint them! All being well, our first team will consist of A. H. Bridger, J. G. Coleman, L. J. Coleman, R. F. Elson, E. C. Heather, S. C. Roberts, W. H. Snell, C. F. Sutton. All are certain to show a high standard of performance, and we have hopes of supplying the individual champion. We shall also have a second team in the field and we can be sure that they will also make a good show. For the benefit of those who do not fully understand the term "Junior" as applied to this race, it is as well to point out that this has nothing to do with age. A member of a winning team; winners of A.A.A. first-class and R.W.A. first-class standard medals; and members of placed teams in the "Senior" 20 Miles Championship (together with one or two other qualifications), debar a walker from competing in the "Junior" Championship. One can always depend upon a good-class field, despite the various barring clauses; and it is the ambition of every walker to obtain his "Junior" gold medal. We hope that our team will receive plenty of support. The ten-mile course is of three laps, and presents plenty of opportunity to see the race. The journey is easily made by Underground to Golders Green station, thence a 1d. bus fare going towards Finchley, to Willifield Way. The dressing rooms will be at the Metropolitan W.C. Headquarters at the Hampstead Garden Suburb Club. We expect to see many Belgrave members there to give an encouraging word to our walkers; and, we trust, to see and help them record the Club's sixth win in this Championship, which carries with it the "Garnet" Cup. * * * * * And meanwhile, what of the Senior 20 Miles Championship to be held on May 14th at Birmingham? This is still the most important event of the Walking calendar, and we hope to succeed in our efforts to take this Championship once again. In recent years the title has eluded us, although we have always been in the placings and on occasions lost the Championship by one and two points only. In 1938 we should like to make the Championship ours again, and we trust all our walkers will consider how they can help to this end. We have the nucleus of a wonderfully good team and with conscientious training and the determined endeavour to do well, nothing can stop us. Up to the time of writing, our season's walking successes have been many, and it would be a very fitting conclusion to the Winter season if we were able to regain the "Senior" Championship. * * * * * It grows more and more obvious year by year that the Boxing Day Godstone-and-back walk of 18¾ miles is misplaced in the present calendar of walking events. It carries, of course, a large amount of traditional interest and as such always commands a fair entry; but it is very doubtful whether many of the entrants train assiduously and show to the best advantage. In fact, a walker intending to follow the season through, from October's 7 miles races to May's 20 miles championship, would be ill-advised to make a special preparation for the Boxing Day race. In the last race held we entered the largest number of any club (with the possible exception of the promoters) and for the first few miles seemed likely winners of the scratch team race. The disqualification of C. E. Churcher, and gradual loss of places by A. H. Bridger as lack of distance training began to tell, dispelled our chances, despite the splendid "second-half" of Jack Bidgood, who eventually finished third. The winner, D. Christie-Murray (S.W.C.) was well away from the others at the finish and recorded 2 hrs. 38 min. 17 sec. for the distance. Our men finished as follows :— Sutton was with the leaders at the half-disance but lost ground later; and one of the pleasing features was the performance of G. S. Doubleday in his first season. The Walking Hon. Secretary has a number of current R.W.A. Handbooks, and these may be had by club-members at 4d. each. * * * * * We understand that England will be represented in the European Games 50 Kilos Walk, to be held in France on September 4th. Bear this date in mind, distance men! * * * * * FROM OUR TRACK CAPTAIN. With one of our most successful Winter seasons almost behind us, we can look forward with anticipation to the Summer fixtures. A full programme of Club handicaps has been arranged, together with our usual Inter-club Scratch Walks, which will take place on Wednesday, June 8th. A big feature of our road success has been the way members have been getting together for training. This is an idea we hope to carry out during the Summer. Collective training every Tuesday, with various packs, will be arranged. It is hoped that a new record will be set up this season in the matter of entries. Bigger fields mean keener racing and an all-round improvement. All the old faces are expected to be seen once more, and, it is hoped, several new ones. It is the duty of every member to see that even the rawest novice gets the encouragement that is so necessary to the beginner. Be ever ready with helpful suggestions and, if in doubt, direct him to the Captain, or any other Club official. Please remember that there is a Captain of the Section for a definite purpose. He is there to give advice, and one should not be nervous of seeking it. * * * * * Enquiries regarding all the various races, scratch and handicap, are welcomed, and every attempt will be made to give the fullest information. So prepare your programme now, and watch yourself progress! * * * * * FUTURE FIXTURES. March 5th—R.W.A. "Junior" Championship at Hampstead Garden Suburb. March 12th—Walk v. Surrey Walking Club : Croydon—Banstead and back (11½ miles). March 19th—Surrey Co. A.A.A. Walk at Wimbledon. Middlesex Co. A.A.A. Walk at Southgate. March 26th—Inter-Counties Walk. items.s: With The Juniors. H. M. Q.'s junior cross-country notes: second in the Surrey County Youths' Race, R. E. Stride winning the Club Junior Championship, second in the Surrey County Junior, and Southern Junior prospects. After an absence of several years we entered, once again, for the Surrey County Youths' Race, held from Belgrave Hall on December 4th. Our boys, many of whom were racing over the country for the first time, were undaunted by the snow and sleet and finished a creditable second. RESULT. On December 18th, the biggest field in recent years turned out for the Club Junior (under 21) Championship. The course was altered slightly to cut out the brook but Stride's time of 29 mins. 15 secs. is, nevertheless, of the same excellent standard set by Stimpson and Clements in previous years. Stride became the holder of the "Savage Shield" with something to spare over W. E. Lucas, but there was some close racing for the minor positions. Beer and Edwards ran very well but Selby was right off form. RESULT. In the Surrey County Junior at Shirley, Mitcham ousted us from our position as holders and hopes that Lucas would bag the individual title were dispelled by the heavy cold which he had. However, our scoring four packed within half-a-minute, enabling us to take second place. Our non-scorers did well in their first attempt at a junior title and should improve considerably with the experience gained. RESULT. Our chances in the Southern Junior are not as bright as they have been in the last two or three years, because Lucas and Stride are both too old. However, Beer, Herbert, Edwards, Selby, Shrubb and Boyden should provide a scoring four capable of being placed. The majority of our other juniors are still under nineteen and with the promise they shew may well provide the club with winning teams in years to come. 1. L. C. Gregory Ranelagh H. 20 15 7. N. C. items.sum: The Track Vice-Captain thanks last season's sprinters for retaining the Inter-Club Relay Shield and calls them to track training at Battersea Park from 5 March 1938.
items.s: Sprinters—A Call to Action! The Track Vice-Captain thanks last season's sprinters for retaining the Inter-Club Relay Shield and calls them to track training at Battersea Park from 5 March 1938. I should like to take this opportunity of thanking all the sprinters who, last season, so ably assisted the Club and, incidentally, whose performances gave me a great deal of encouragement in my first year as a Track Vice-Captain. Last season was the most successful for several seasons, as far as the sprinters were concerned. The performances were good and will improve a great deal with correct training and encouragement. The team spirit was a revelation to me. I felt I could always rely on the sprinters turning out. This trust was proved by the section being, so to speak, self-supporting. I think I am correct when I say that last season was the first for many years when the Club has not had to call on members from other sections of the Club to gain points for us in the Inter-Club Relay Shield. I write these next few words without a blush. The sprinters laid the foundation of a record number of points win to retain the Shield. These races proved to me that the right spirit is in all of you. Reserves were quite prepared to travel with the team; and in this respect I would like to thank Frank Simmonds for his good sportsmanship. Enough said about last season. Let us now start seriously training for an even more strenuous track season. The next two months are those in which we can gain a solid foundation in the shape of a fit body. Study your exercises and remember that concentration on the benefit of a particular exercise is the keynote to happy training. Stomach, leg, arm and chest exercises should be started, and adhered to morning and night, increasing in intensity as the body is strengthened. I am looking forward to meeting you all again, and March 5th, 1938, has been chosen as the first Saturday of track training for 1938 at Battersea Park, at 3 p.m. I appeal to you all, Seniors and Juniors, to support me on this date, as during training I wish to discuss with you our plans for 1938. Results last year proved that there is real talent in this section of the Club. Messrs. Botwright, Blunden, Pritchard, Skelley and others will all improve with experience. We (the Belgrave Harriers) would also like to see some of the older members back in training, such as Messrs. Bone, Mewes, Kealey and Co. The Club has many promising juniors also. As I have already mentioned, Juniors will be very welcome on March 5th, and I can assure them I will do all I can to put them on the right road. Come along on March 5th and ask as many questions as you like. One last word. Get your new shoes NOW, or have your present ones repaired so that they are comfortable for training. Here's wishing you the best-ever season for 1938! L. G. Bennett L. G. items.sum: Look back at club walking and cross-country results of late 1927 and early 1928 as reported ten years earlier.
items.s: Ten Years Back. Look back at club walking and cross-country results of late 1927 and early 1928 as reported ten years earlier. Let's glance at our "Belgravian" of ten years ago and see what was happening at the close of 1927, and in the early days of 1928. Our Junior Walking Championship for the "Horwood" Cup, was won by J. G. Scammell, with F. H. Elson and S. L. King in the minor positions; and on the same day the 7 miles Cross-country Championship was won by Arthur Clark from E. A. Duffett and W. A. Rice. This latter race was held in conjunction with an inter-club event v. S. George's Services S.C. 34 finished the course, and the placed men in the handicap were F. G. Ford, A. Traquair and A. A. Harley. Duffett was placed third in the Surrey County Cross-country Championship, running as an individual; and our scoring team on that day was H. E. Footer (6), A. D. Pyer (7), A. E. Smith (14), H. S. Cook (20), W. L. Bayliss (23), J. D. Andrews (26). The 10 miles C.C. Championship was contested by 21 starters and provided A. Clark with another win. Duffett and Pyer were second and third; with W. G. Webb (fourth in the scratch race) the sealed handicap winner. T. W. Green, A. L. Fletcher, R. D. McMullen were first three in the 10 miles Walk; the handicap first prize going to J. E. Field. The following paragraph, abstracted from our Gazette of ten years ago, gives some idea of the improvement since made. It reads: "At long last! Twenty-four years ago we gained third place in the South of the Thames Championship, and this year the performance has been repeated." A. Robertshaw, H. E. Footer, P. Khlopin, W. G. Webb, A. D. Pyer and W. L. Bayliss formed the team. In the "Southern" we had hopes of being placed for the first time, but the best we could do was tenth with 422 points! The race, held at Shenfield, was won by H. W. Payne; and our scoring team men were H. E. Footer (33), W. G. Webb (37), P. Khlopin (38), A. D. Pyer (56), W. S. Mitchell (125), A. Clark (133). In the "National," held at Leamington in a snowstorm, our position was 17th of the 27 teams. Bill Webb was our first man home in 63rd position. In 1928, the R.W.A. Junior Championship was held at Wembley and there were 238 starters. Sheffield United Harriers were the winners; and our team was third, the scoring team being Scammell (12th), F. H. Elson (17th), J. E. Field (22nd) and Carne (24th). These were the happenings that stirred us ten years ago! J. G. Scammell J. G. items.label: June 1938
items.sum: Editorial notes celebrating the walkers' unprecedented treble of R.W.A. Junior, 20 Miles and 50 Kilos championships, with notes on the runners' season, the track season, the W. A. Rice Memorial Trophy, the A.A.A. 10 miles run and 7 miles walk, the Dinner-Dance and Fred Bentley's England selection.
items.s: Editorial notes celebrating the walkers' unprecedented treble of R.W.A. Junior, 20 Miles and 50 Kilos championships, with notes on the runners' season, the track season, the W. A. Rice Memorial Trophy, the A.A.A. 10 miles run and 7 miles walk, the Dinner-Dance and Fred Bentley's England selection. Since our last issue appeared the principal events of the Winter Season have been decided, and the Track Season run part of its course. The accomplishment which must command our attention above all other matters, and merits our sincerest congratulation, is that of our walkers in winning the R.W.A. 10 Miles "Junior" Championship, R.W.A. 20 Miles Championship and R.W.A. 50 Kilos. Championship. No other club has ever at any time won all three championships; and to do so in the space of three months is almost miraculous. This record of success is one that may never again be approached by any club, and we most heartily congratulate and thank the members of the winning teams. * * * * * The performance of Colin Sutton in appearing in all three championship teams is one that may never be equalled. He was sixth in the "Junior," fourth in the 20 Miles Championship, and fifth in the 50 Kilos' Championship—a trio of performances that reflect the greatest credit on Colin's conscientious training and determined efforts to help the Club to a treble victory. Others deserving our congratulations are Fred Bentley, who was placed second in both 20 Miles and 50 Kilos. events; and to Joe Coleman and Len Coleman, who dead-heated in the "Junior" Championship for first place. It is interesting to note that as a result of the Winter season's activities, all five trophies which the Road Walking Association offer for competition (the "National" Shield, "Garnet" Cup, "Horlick" Cup, "Nijmegen" Shield and "Berman" Cup) are in the possession of the Belgrave Harriers! Our runners have not won Championships, but have certainly maintained the high standard they have set themselves in recent years. The "Southern" was lost by a single point; and we claimed third position in both the "National" and the Brighton Relay—all performances of real merit! Our record of being placed in the English Cross-Country Championship for six consecutive years is one of which we are very proud, and one we hope to add to for many years to come. * * * * * The track season has opened well, many successes being recorded. We are particularly pleased with our success at Reading in our first attempt to gain the "Evening Gazette" Trophy; and at the success of our walkers in the Inter-Club Scratch Walks. * * * * * It is proposed to close the "W. A. Rice Memorial Trophy" subscription list at the end of the month, and those who have not done so, and would like to be associated with the idea, are asked to get in touch with Mr. A. A. Harley at once. * * * * * Our Hon. Treasurer has Club ties, vests, etc., and would be pleased to supply you upon request. He also awaits a few outstanding subscriptions, and if you have been remiss in this, your prompt attention would be appreciated. * * * * * Please note that our worthy President and Hon. Secretary has changed his address (see page 1); and see that you make a note of this to avoid delays in correspondence. * * * * * Our Club gave better support than any other to the A.A.A. 10 Miles Run and 7 Miles Walking Championships held on April 23rd; and our boys were very prominent. In the Walk J. G. Coleman finished third, the first Englishman to finish, L. J. Coleman was fifth and D. E. Brown seventh. In the Run, A. W. Penny was third, C. T. Carter fourth, and S. T. Ring twelfth, all inside first-class standard time. * * * * * Although held on the same day as the Brighton Relay, our Dinner-Dance, held at Gatti's Adelaide Restaurant, was well attended and a distinct success. Our thanks are due to A. E. Taylor for making all the necessary arrangements. * * * * * Fred Bentley did well to improve upon record in the Police Barking—Southend Championship; and we congratulate him upon being selected to represent England in France on June 19th. Murphy" Shield, held with an inter-club match against the Metropolitan Police and Surrey A.C., won by Harry Churcher. Second-placed J. G. Coleman's net time is printed as 89 39 although 82 39 less 2 0 gives 80 39. This Club Championship for the "R. Murphy" Shield was held on January 29th, when we also entertained the Metropolitan Police and Surrey A.C. in an inter-club event. Right from the start Belgrave led, followed by a batch, many of whom, whilst unyielding in their allegiance to the Club, become "the enemy" also on two or three occasions a year. Harry Churcher maintained his excellent form and proved that the ten miles distance is not beyond him, in winning this championship for the first time by nearly two minutes from "Junior" Joe Coleman, with Percy Wright third. Then came many of our younger walkers consolidating their claims to places in the Club "Junior" team a few weeks later. Right well did they do so; and this race, as apparently do all races these days, once again showed the strength of Belgrave. It was very pleasing to see such a fine field out. Handicap awards went to R. F. Elson, A. H. Bridger and E. C. Heather; and a glance at the appended result will show that our walkers meant "business" on this last Saturday in January. RESULTS. 1 H. items.label: June 1938
items.sum: P. G. Wright's report on the R.W.A. "Junior" 10 miles championship from Hampstead, where the Coleman brothers dead-heated for first and Belgrave won the team title with a record 16 points, with results and team placings.
items.s: The R.W.A. "Junior" Championship. P. G. Wright's report on the R.W.A. "Junior" 10 miles championship from Hampstead, where the Coleman brothers dead-heated for first and Belgrave won the team title with a record 16 points, with results and team placings. Beautiful weather and our own club red hot favourites. it was not surprising a large number of supporters travelled Hampstead way for the National "Junior" 10 Miles Championship. Held from the headquarters of the holders, Metropolitan W.C., we had every hope of supplying both team and individual winners. Right from the start the Coleman brothers went to the front, and began to open up a big lead. At first Heaney, of Lancashire W.C., endeavoured to go with them, but he was well short of the necessary pace. Jim Fisher the big Surrey walker, got to within thirty yards at eight miles, but his effort began to tell and he dropped back. Joe with his "I'm his big brother" smile; and Len (not so small brother, look !) came in together on their own. (Work it out !—Ed.). It was a brilliant performance. Len has been walking less than two years, but Joe has now been at the game several seasons. Only hard work and a terrific keenness could have secured Joe the joint title, as he is not a natural walker in physique. Our third man to finish, Colin Sutton, walked through fast towards the end, after being well behind at the beginning of the race. He was closely followed by Reg. Elson, the team returning a new record score of 16 points. Eddie Heather was well to the front at the start,but went back as his early pace began to tell. Bridger will be a big asset next year, as should "Marathon Doub," who surprised everyone with a brilliant performance. Sympathy must be extended to Roberts who after a hectic taxi ride to arrive on time, suffered disqualification. The second team's performance in finishing so well up (5th) was a delight to everyone, and I feel sure that the Bels. can view next year's race with eager anticipation, especially when one remembers that we shall be strengthened by Bert Clayton, our Eastleigh walker. e: Belgrave Harriers v Surrey Walking Club
items.s: Match v. Surrey Walking Club. Report and result of the match against Surrey Walking Club over their Banstead and back course (11½ miles), won by Belgrave with Joe Coleman first. The week following the "Junior" we tried conclusions with our S.W.C. friends, over their Banstead and back course (11½ miles) and scored a win with ten walking aside. Joe Coleman again distinguished himself by winning easily, with plenty in hand, only to find he was but a few seconds outside record for the course. Sound team work gave us a good win over the Surrey W.C., whom we are always glad to meet, and always glad to beat; for then we know we have indeed accomplished a good performance. items.label: June 1938
items.sum: Report on the Surrey county walk championship, where Joe Coleman won and Belgrave took the team trophy for the first time, the Middlesex championship where Cadogan A.C. were second to Metropolitan W.C., and Alan Bridger's Kent 10 miles title.
items.s: The County Walk Championships. Report on the Surrey county walk championship, where Joe Coleman won and Belgrave took the team trophy for the first time, the Middlesex championship where Cadogan A.C. were second to Metropolitan W.C., and Alan Bridger's Kent 10 miles title. The Surrey race was held from our quarters at Wimbledon, and although we approached this race with greater confidence than ever before, in the expectation of winning a championship that had hitherto eluded us, the Judges almost won, only 20 of the 34 starters finishing! Harry Churcher suffered disqualification when in possession of a comfortable lead at 8½ miles, and brother Charlie also failed to finish. Fortunately, Joe Coleman was there to win the individual championship, with Len second and, with the assistance of Don Brown and Jack Field, the team trophy was ours for the first time. Now we have it after years of trying, we hope to retain the title for some years. 1. Belgrave Harriers (1, 2, 6, 9) ... 18 pts. 2. Surrey W.C. (3, 4, 7, 8) ... 22 pts. * * * * * On the same day the Middlesex Championship was held from Enfield West over an undulating course. Percy Wright held the lead for some miles but eventually was challenged by H. H. Whitlock, who went on to win from our man by 19 seconds. The team race was keenly fought out between Cadogan A.C., comprised of Belgrave Harriers possessing Middlesex qualifications, and the holders, Metropolitan W.C. The holders retained their title, scoring 27 points to the 32 of Cadogan. Colin Sutton finished fifth, but was not eligible for team competition this year (this also applies to J. C. Bidgood) and the absence of W. A. Treacher made an undoubted difference. Next season our boys hope to annex this title. This year's team to take second medals was : P. G. Wright, F. E. Bentley, A. Readman, R. F. Elson. * * * * * Congratulations to Alan Bridger upon winning the Kent 10 miles title. We expect him to be in a winning "Junior" team next year. Field's net time (3 5 29 less 15 30 = 2 49 59) is given as 2 49 10, and G. H. Boddington's allowance as 22 39 though his net time implies 22 30. The race to decide who should hold the "R.W. Ricketts" Shield and match event versus Metropolitan Police, attracted a good entry. As usual, there were many retirements. The Club Championship found a new holder, Colin Sutton being first man home. He walked with both power and speed, and although a very tired man towards the finish, he lasted home and showed that we have another first-class distance walker in our ranks. Jack Bidgood gave his usual sound display in second place, and Charlie Churcher, the holder, finished third. Of the younger walkers, Jack Rutland and Reg Elson both gave sound performances. Rutland would have done even better if he had not been in the lead early on, and when experience brings more knowledge of even pace, we may expect an outstanding performance from him. Bentley and Rickards were among those who retired, but we are always assured of a first-rate performance from these two loyal team men when the National Championship comes along. items.sum: Report and Belgrave results of the annual Colchester to Ipswich 17 miles walk, won in record time by Colin Sutton, with Belgrave "A" winning the team race.
items.s: Colchester to Ipswich. Report and Belgrave results of the annual Colchester to Ipswich 17 miles walk, won in record time by Colin Sutton, with Belgrave "A" winning the team race. A good party of Belgrave walkers took advantage of the courtesy of the Metropolitan Police W.C. to share in the coach which they had arranged; to visit the Eastern Counties and take part in the annual 17 miles walk. From the start (where we were glad to see K. N. Wood, now resident at Colchester) our walkers went to the front and team honours were always safe in our keeping. A strong head wind all the way caused much inconvenience, but did not prevent Colin Sutton from winning in record time. He was closely followed by Bob Readman, who was also placed second in the sealed handicap. Third to finish was Jack Bidgood, and our team was completed by Captain Charlie Churcher in fifth position, and we had six in nine. Joe Coleman made his first attempt at a distance race, and was prominent for several miles, but lack of preparation for this distance (a week after the A.A.A. 7 Miles Championship) caused him to fall back towards the end. However, it is certain that he is capable of a really first-class performance in the longer races; and we expect him to be as prominent at 20 miles in a year or so's time as he has proved himself this season in the shorter events. Harry Thaxter did well to finish 12th—our eighth man! Had either Coleman or Rutland been declared as a "B" team man, we should have taken another set of awards, but we must not be too greedy! items.label: June 1938
items.sum: Report and result of the R.W.A. 20 miles championship at Birmingham, regained by Belgrave with a club-best 23 points plus the "Nijmegen" Shield, Fred Bentley second to J. Hopkins. The team result prints Belgrave "B" as 10th with 296 pts., more than the 211 of 11th-placed Woodford Green A.C.
items.s: The R.W.A. 20 Miles Championship. Report and result of the R.W.A. 20 miles championship at Birmingham, regained by Belgrave with a club-best 23 points plus the "Nijmegen" Shield, Fred Bentley second to J. Hopkins. The team result prints Belgrave "B" as 10th with 296 pts., more than the 211 of 11th-placed Woodford Green A.C. May 14th, 1938, was a great day for the Club, for we regained, in decisive manner, the Championship which we last held in 1929. In the eight intervening years we have gained second place three times, and third medals on three occasions; so our win was all the sweeter on this second Saturday in May. And now as to the manner of our fifth Championship win at this distance. The race, held from Cape End, Birmingham, started in slight rain, which persisted for some time but did not prove any great inconvenience. At five miles Surrey W.C. and Leicester W.C. were both ahead of us in points, but the race had only just begun. At ten miles our men were picking up valuable points, and now we held a slight lead from Leicester and S.W.C. At 13 miles H. W. Whitlock was disqualified, and J. Hopkins, of Lancashire W.C., led, followed by our Fred Bentley. Colin Sutton was fourth, and we had several men between tenth and twentieth positions. The scoring was now: Belgrave 25 pts., Surrey W.C. 38 pts., Leicester 50 pts. Over the last five miles of the race, Leicester tried hard to get on terms with our boys, but without effect. Jack Bidgood and Fred Rickards showed their experience of previous tussles, and relentlessly carried through, holding off all challengers, and even picking up a few points. So came the end, with our scoring four finishing in the first nine positions, giving a total of 23 points—a Club "best." This was generally acknowledged to be one of the finest team efforts in the history of the Championship, and our walkers deserve our thanks and heartiest congratulations. Leicester W.C., with 34 points, were a worthy second team. Their low score was six points better than when they dead-heated for the title last year, and much higher scores have frequently won the championship. Third came our Surrey Walking Club friends with 55 points, relegated from the very high standard they have set themselves in recent years, but we may be sure that they will come again. Of those other than the scoring team, Charlie Churcher and Bob Readman were always handy, ready to make a really big effort if called upon. Jack Rutland and Joe Coleman, both taking part in their first "National," performed creditably and gained experience, which will probably take them into the first 20 placings another year. The efforts of our team of eight gained for the Club the "Nijmegen" Shield, which is presented to the first team to finish its complete team of eight. Well done! We have previously only won this Shield once—in 1933. Our "B" team may also be considered to have done well in finishing tenth, and beating the first choice of such clubs as Woodford Green A.C., Metropolitan W.C., Derbyshire S.C., London Vidarians W.C., Highgate H. and others. Bob Martin, Syd Roberts and Harry Thaxter even beat our eighth "A" team man. Altogether, we look back with profound satisfaction on this Championship Day. A special word of praise is due to Fred Bentley on his second position, and to Colin Sutton on finishing fourth, and thereby winning his Club Honours Badge. We are glad to hold again the "National" Shield and the "Nijmegen" Shield, in addition to the "Garnett" Cup, which the "Juniors" won with a record score two months earlier. As ever, the obligations of the Champions are to defend—to withstand the challengers—and next season we hope to do this successfully. RESULT. 115 were timed in. TEAM RESULT. items.s: The R.W.A. 50 Kilos. Championship. Report and result of the R.W.A. 50 kilometres championship at Bradford, the club's third walking championship of the season, won by Belgrave with Fred Bentley second to the Olympic champion H. H. Whitlock, plus a tribute to Fred Rickards. The crowning effort of the season, and our third Championship win, took place at Bradford on Whit Monday. Five men—F. E. Bentley, C. F. Sutton, F. Rickards, R. Martin and A. Readman—represented us over this most difficult course of 31 1-8 miles, and all finished, bringing further distinction to the Club. A team victory was always assured, for our men were prominent from the start. Both Bentley and Sutton led the field at one time or another, and Rickards was always in the first ten placings. The great feature of the race was the tussle which developed between the Olympic champion and our Fred Bentley. With the possibility of International selection for the European Games next September to spur them on, both men gave of their best. Eventually Whitlock's superior knowledge of the course, over which he has won many races, prevailed and enabled him to beat Fred by something under 100 yards. Both men had hard races and showed excellent form, and England should have no cause for complaint if these two do duty for her at Paris on September 4th. Colin Sutton walked splendidly once again to finish fifth. What a wonderful season he has had! Fred Rickards, a few seconds later, in sixth place, completed our team. Fred, at the age of 39, is in his 24th season of walking, and still he remains one of the best in the country. His sportsmanship, too, is second to none, and we are glad to have such a man as a Life Member of the Club and as a member of our teams. We are sure he is good for many more years yet, and we are indeed grateful to him for his assistance and the spirit he has helped to instil among our younger walkers. Three championships in one season has, at times, seemed an almost unattainable ideal; but now it has been accomplished. Our thanks are due to all who have helped in this accomplishment. It is not given to all to score for the Club, or even represent the Club; but to the many who have contributed their quota, to those who have given encouragement and helped things along, we express our thanks. items.s: With the Walkers. Walking notes: appeal for new members and the novices' one mile walk, the club's championship record, walkers converted from running and cycling, the "Leicester Mercury" 20 miles walk, the club championship at Tooting Bec and an extra three miles race with Surrey Walking Club. As mentioned elsewhere, our last few months' activities have largely consisted of successes and still more successes. Everyone has done something towards these achievements, and with several promising walkers showing improvement, we hope to carry on in the winning way. At the height of success it is always as well to consider the future—and the future is dependent upon the influx of the right type of new member. Given an average physique and the intention to persevere and overcome the initial difficulties which come to all of us, we can almost guarantee some measure of success. We trust all members will do their best to introduce new talent, and here we would remind everyone of our One Mile Walk for unattached novices (entry free) on July 20th. * * * * * We have won the "Junior" Championship in 1920, 1922, 1930, 1933, 1936 and 1938. The 20 Miles title has been ours in 1924, 1925, 1928, 1929 and again this year; and we have held the "Horlick" Cup for the 50 kilos. Championship in 1934, 1935, 1936 and 1938. We are the only Club to have held all three Championships; and now we are proud to have improved even upon this by taking all three titles in one season. * * * * * A feature of the season has been the success of some of our walkers who have previously tried themselves out at other branches of sport. Thus both of the Colemans had been in the running ranks for some years. Doubleday is another to have changed over and shows great promise; while in Colin Sutton we have one who has competed with some distinction in cycling road races. Maybe there are others who could turn to walking and make a success of it, as have many of our stalwarts in the past. * * * * * A team, unfortunately far from our strongest, competed in the "Leicester Mercury" 20 Miles Walk. Fred Rickards was 4th 2hr. 53min. 20sec.), Rutland 10th (3hr. 1min. 4sec.), Sutton 13th (3hr. 3min. 10sec.), and Doubleday 42nd. Our team placing was 5th. Next season we hope to arrange for a stronger team to travel and score our first win in this race. * * * * * All walkers should have the Summer fixture lists and it should not be necessary to detail the future events here. We would draw particular attention, however, to the Club Championship to be held at Tooting Bec Track on Saturday, July 30th. * * * * * All entries for Club events and requests for information to— A. A. Harley, 39, Roxborough Avenue, Isleworth, Mx. * * * * * ADDITIONAL FIXTURE.—We have accepted an invitation from Surrey Walking Club to take part in a Three Miles race at Tooting Bec Track, on Wednesday, July 6th, at 8 p.m. This is to be an "all-to-score" affair, and it is hoped that all our members, from the fastest to the slowest, will support the event.
